articles.title: Amazon hires a veteran Microsoft AI leader to help build its tools for coding and work
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A longtime Microsoft engineering leader who was previously a Copilot chief technology officer is joining Amazon Web Services to work on its competing AI tools for coding and workplace productivity.

Pedram Rezaei , a nearly 20-year Microsoft veteran who was most recently a corporate vice president on the Microsoft Superintelligence team, starts Monday as a distinguished engineer in the AWS Agentic AI and Emerging Technologies organization, led by Swami Sivasubramanian.

Rezaei will work initially on Kiro, the AWS coding tool, and Quick, Amazon’s AI assistant for workplace tasks, Sivasubramanian wrote in a memo to his team Monday. “He is a hands-on engineer who is still in the code every day, and he plans to keep it that way here,” he added.

Kiro’s user count doubled from the first quarter to the second, and monthly AI users for Quick grew fourfold, according to the memo. Rezaei’s plan for his first few months is to “meet people, learn how things work here, and ship something real,” Sivasubramanian wrote.
Sivasubramanian’s organization was expanded in July to include emerging technologies, part of a broader reshuffling of Amazon’s AI teams.

The hire comes as Amazon and Microsoft compete more directly in AI tools for work. Microsoft last month unveiled an all-in-one Copilot app that combines chat, coding and agents, its answer to OpenAI and Anthropic. Amazon made its Quick desktop app generally available in September and brought its main features to mobile.

Rezaei joined Microsoft in 2006 and held senior technical roles on Power BI, Dynamics 365, Cortana, Bing and Azure Maps before moving to Copilot, according to his LinkedIn profile . He became Copilot’s CTO in February and moved to the Microsoft Superintelligence team in June, according to the profile. Sivasubramanian’s memo said Rezaei was most recently working on training foundation models.
We’ve contacted Microsoft for comment on his departure.
Rezaei is the latest Microsoft executive to move to AWS this year. Shawn Bice returned to AWS in May from a security role at Microsoft to lead its Automated Reasoning Group.

In his memo Monday, Sivasubramanian also told his team that two longtime AWS engineers, Marvin Theimer and Reto Kramer , have returned to work on neurosymbolic AI and automated reasoning, which he called “one of our biggest bets for the future.” Both came back from Microsoft, according to their LinkedIn profiles.
Neurosymbolic AI pairs large language models with rule-based systems that can check whether an AI agent is following a company’s policies and procedures.

Speaking at Madrona’s IA40 Summit in Seattle last week, Sivasubramanian said nearly every CIO and CEO raises the same question about AI agents. “How do I know it is always going to obey all my rules and regulations?” he said. “This is a real concern.”
Solving that problem “actually unlocks so many use cases for all these enterprises,” he added.

Theimer, an AWS distinguished engineer for nine years before leaving in 2022, joined Microsoft in July 2024 as a corporate vice president and technical architect and stayed until March. It was his second stint at the company, where he worked from 1998 to 2006. He rejoined AWS in July as a vice president and distinguished engineer.

Kramer, who led an automated reasoning team at AWS before leaving in 2023, joined Microsoft in September 2025 as vice president of Security Platform & AI and stayed until May. He rejoined AWS in September as vice president of applied science.
Sivasubramanian hinted at more hires to come, writing that Rezaei joins “as we continue to build out our technical leadership team to help take on the ambitious work we have planned.”

articles.title: Seattle’s tax burden shifted to business as jobs slipped away, new report finds
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Seattle’s tax collections have nearly tripled over the past decade, soaring from $900 million in 2013 to a projected $2.8 billion in 2026. But who pays those taxes, and how the tax revenue is collected, looks vastly different today than a decade ago.

A new report released by ECOnorthwest, commissioned jointly by the Downtown Seattle Association (DSA) and the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, show city tax revenues far outstripping population and job growth, driven by targeted corporate taxes on a small pool of major employers.

Between 2013 and 2025, Seattle’s tax revenues jumped 172%, outpacing population growth (31%), job growth (23%), and local inflation (50%) . During that period, real tax growth grew 5.6 times faster than population and 7.5 times faster than employment .

The findings come as city leaders, major tech employers and regional business groups grapple with shifting post-pandemic work patterns and a political climate that has frequently placed large technology companies like Amazon in its sights.

According to the report, broad-based core taxes, such as property, sales, utility, and general Business & Occupation (B&O) taxes, comprised 83% of city tax collections in 2013. By 2026, those core broad taxes are projected to drop to just 52% of the total revenue.
Replacing them are narrow, targeted tax levies :

Combined, two taxes that did not exist five years ago now account for nearly a third of all business tax dollars collected by the city. Overlap among top taxpayers means fewer than 20 companies account for roughly $356 million in annual City of Seattle revenue.

“Seattle’s tax collections are growing far faster than its population, jobs or inflation. Employers are carrying more of that burden. That trajectory is not sustainable,” said Seattle Metro Chamber president & CEO Joe Nguyen. “The question cannot always be how to collect more money. It must be how to deliver better results with the money we already have and build a tax structure that helps our economy grow.”
The heavy pivot to business revenue coincides with divergent employment trends between Seattle and its neighboring Eastside hubs .

Between March 2020 and March 2025, Seattle lost approximately 24,000 jobs, while the remainder of King County added 21,000. The report notes that Seattle lost 18,000 jobs in the single year leading up to March 2025 alone. And that figure that does not yet capture the full impact of major remote work policies and tech layoffs announced across the region.

The report arrives on the heels of previous GeekWire coverage tracking regional tech dynamics, including the shift of high tech jobs from Seattle to Bellevue , as well as broader political shifts in how West Coast hubs are responding to tech sector backlash and the AI boom .

However, in a sign that Mayor Katie Wilson is paying close attention to tech-sector headwinds and shifting job patterns, she proposed a $9.1 billion 2027 budget that would erase a $175 million general fund deficit and cut nearly $50 million in spending while freezing JumpStart tax rates.

articles.title: Orbital Robotics gets set to send up a pair of arms for International Space Station’s robots
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: A free-flying NASA robot aboard the International Space Station will soon demonstrate a system for capturing and servicing satellites in orbit, using a pair of autonomous robotic arms built by Seattle startup Orbital Robotics .

“This demo will prove our ability to capture, manipulate and upgrade satellites on orbit, moving humanity one massive step forward towards reusable satellites,” Orbital Robotics CEO Aaron Borger said today in a news release.

Borger told GeekWire that the company plans to send its robotic arms to the space station in the third quarter of 2027. Three separate demonstrations would be conducted, each about a month apart, he said.

The mission will mark a major milestone for Orbital Robotics, which was founded in 2024 by Borger and other veterans of Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture, including lead hardware engineer Riley Mark, lead software engineer Sohil Pokharna and adviser Doug Kohl. Orbital Robotics has been developing arms controlled by artificial intelligence for use on free-flying spacecraft, and this will be the company’s first opportunity to prove out its capture technology and autonomous control software together in microgravity under real spaceflight conditions.

The demonstration is a joint effort with Arkisys, NASA’s sustaining and maintenance partner for the Astrobee program, which will provide integration support and in-space platform infrastructure. A successful demo would boost confidence that free-flying robots equipped with Orbital Robotics’ arms could conduct satellite servicing missions.

“Free flight proves you can get there, manipulation proves you can do something once you arrive,” Arkisys CEO David Barnhart said. “Pairing Astrobee with Orbital Robotics’ arms creates a powerful proxy for the servicing and assembly operations that will shape the future ISAM [in-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing] economy.”

Three cube-shaped Astrobee robots — nicknamed Bumble, Queen and Honey — are currently available for testing aboard the ISS. In 2024, one of the Astrobees was outfitted with a set of tentacle-like arms that grabbed onto a boxy cube to demonstrate the system’s gripping ability. Borger said the Orbital Robotics / Arkisys demo would be similar to the tentacle test.
Orbital Robotics’ arms for the Astrobee demonstration will be scaled-down versions of the ORA-A arm that the company has built in its Seattle lab, Borger said.

“The arms will be sent up to the ISS and then installed onto one of the Astrobees by the crew,” Borger said in an email. “The Astrobee with the arms will then demonstrate the capture and servicing on a second Astrobee that is already on the ISS. … After the capture, we will replace a simple compute module we will launch and integrate with the Astrobee being captured.”

Borger said the ISS demonstration is an internally funded program. “We are paying for the launch and demonstrations with Arkisys as our implementation partner through their Space Act Agreement with NASA,” he said.

After the demonstration, the arms will remain available aboard the ISS to assist astronauts with moving cargo, to automate simple tasks involving robotic manipulation, and to provide opportunities for roboticists to conduct follow-up experiments.

NASA and its commercial partners are already preparing for the next step in space robotics: The Fly Foundational Robots mission , due for launch in late 2027, will deploy a satellite equipped with a commercial robotic arm for demonstrations of in-space servicing tasks.

articles.title: Ballard Link Community Forum on October 19
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Seattle City Councilmember (District 6) and Sound Transit Boardmember Dan Strauss is hosting a community form discussing the Ballard Link Extension alongside several other elected officials and Sound Transit representatives. The forum will be held in the Osberg Great Hall at the National Nordic Museum on Monday, October 19, from 6-8pm .

In a newsletter emailed to constituents last week, Dan Strauss announced the event while highlighting his efforts to get Sound Transit to commit to building the full Ballard Link Extension to Market Street. These included requiring Sound Transit staff to determine when the agency would be able to complete the Ballard Link Extension under current conditions, and looking for ways to reduce project costs in order to open the extension sooner. Currently, the agency expects to open the SODO to Seattle Center portion of the Ballard Link Extension in 2042.

In July, Sound Transit fulfilled Strauss’ first requirement with the announcement the rest of the project could be delayed to 2060 unless significant cost savings are found. When voters passed ST3 in 2016, the entire Ballard Link Extension was expected to open in 2035. In 2021, this schedule slipped to 2037 or 2039 as Sound Transit realized the cost to build a second Link-only tunnel under downtown and managing other complications would far exceed expectations . After calculating “bottom-up” cost estimates for the proposed design of the extension last year, the agency found the full project could cost nearly twice its previous estimate. Compounded with exploding cost estimates across ST3, the Sound Transit Board voted to defer construction of line past Seattle Center until costs were reduced or additional revenue were found.

Sound Transit says it may be able to open the full extension in 2042 if the agency can reduce the total estimated cost by $1 billion (or identify that much in new revenue), begin acquiring property by 2030, finish design by 2032, and lock in funding to start construction by 2033. Regardless, Ballard Link advocates remain dedicated to pushing Sound Transit to return to the originally promised date of opening in 2035.

At the community forum, Sound Transit is expected to share more about its proposed timeline for the Ballard Link Extension, the work agency staff have been doing to reduce costs, and its next steps for the project. There will also be a Q&A session.

Those interested in a seat should probably arrive early. The National Nordic Museum is located at the intersection of 28th Ave NW and NW Market Street, just under a mile west of the planned terminus of the Ballard Link Extension. Nearby bus stops are served by King County Metro Routes 17 and 44 .

articles.title: Deadline Approaches for Outside Ideas to Curb Costs on Ballard Light Rail
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: The due date is approaching for engineering firms to submit cost-saving ideas for the Ballard Link light rail extension, but some transit advocates are criticizing Sound Transit's process and questioning whether the agency is actually open to new ideas and innovative approaches.

Many Sound Transit 3 (ST3) expansion projects are facing headwinds, but Ballard Link in particular faces considerable uncertainty, with a 2042 opening date for the whole line the best case scenario, which would require closing a huge budget gap of around $8 billion. The less-rosy scenario would be opening only the portion through Downtown Seattle in the 2040s and delaying the Interbay and Ballard section to the 2060s , allowing more time for funding to accrue in Sound Transit's coffers. West Seattle Link, meanwhile, has slipped to 2035 – five years later than initially envisioned.

When the Sound Transit Board of Directors overhauled project schedules on May 28, it established a Request for Information (RFI) process to solicit cost-effective design ideas for Ballard Link from outside firms. However that RFI didn't actually go out the door until last month. Sound Transit issued the RFI on September 2, with responses due October 5. That deadline has since been extended a week to October 12.

Advocates with the Save Ballard Rail coalition pushed for the RFI and hoped that it would open the door to much more cost-effective approaches that allow Sound Transit to deliver light rail to Ballard closer to its original timeline in the 2030s.

One of those cost-slashing ideas was converting Ballard Link to an automated light rail (ALR) system with shorter trains and stations, as proposed in a white paper by former Seattle Department of Transportation director Scott Kubly and transportation planner Trevor Reed, and popularized in an Urbanist op-ed . Copenhagen used this technology to overcome their own financial crisis and deliver a highly successful metro system, providing a proof of concept, but the authors do not think Sound Transit is taking their idea seriously.

"They have structured an RFI process that is almost guaranteed to validate their current approach," Kubly and Reed told The Urbanist in a joint written response. "They did no industry outreach ahead of time, they barely publicized the RFI, and they gave an extremely abbreviated response period. This is not the approach of a competent agency or an agency that wants serious responses. This is a clear example of a bureaucratic following the letter but not the spirit of a board request."

Another idea that has garnered interest from Save Ballard Rail and other transit groups is exploring elevated rail as a means to avoid incurring huge costs digging a deep tunnel and cavernous stations in downtown Seattle. Civil engineer Travis Henderson pitched the idea in a white paper he sent to Sound Transit this spring and finetuned in an op-ed in The Urbanist last month. Several transit groups endorsed studying the idea, including Seattle Subway and Transit Equity for All.

"Against a 34-year wait until 2060 for the full line, two or three years of further study is not the risk. The current plan is," Henderson wrote. "Declining to study an alternative with $10 billion in potential savings because the analysis may cost tens of millions is not sound process management. It is institutional inertia, a sunk-cost fallacy that completes the paperwork for a tunnel Sound Transit cannot afford to build, while blocking the alternatives most likely to reach Ballard."

Henderson pointed out the parameters of the RFI precluded firms from putting forward elevated rail as a replacement for planned tunnel sections downtown. The RFI instructs respondents that they "must be mindful of the existing project definition and eschew strategies that could further jeopardize the project timeline." Since Sound Transit has never formally studied elevated rail for the downtown section, it does not fit the project definition.
In a series of Bluesky posts , Kubly criticized how quietly Sound Transit was conducting the RFI process.

"Thursday before Labor Day they issue [the RFI], wait 1.5 weeks to publicize, give 30 days to respond," Kubly wrote. "It’s almost as if they don’t want serious responses. Their staff wrote a memo in April reviewing our proposal. Tips their hand that they aren’t receptive to new ideas."

Kubly also questioned whether agency staff had given automated light rail proposal a fair shot. Sound Transit's deputy executive director for enterprise planning, Alex Krieg, quietly issued an internal memo responding to Kubly and Reed's proposal in April, but the agency didn't send it to the authors or the outside world until June 12 – after the board had voted on the financial plan.

The memo poo-poos the savings possible with shorter choo choos, claiming Kubly and Reed overestimated how large planned stations are likely to be. Additionally, Krieg argued Seattle costs are uniquely driven up by high seismic risk and the earthquake-proofing requirements that brings related to liquefaction risk and unfavorable soil conditions (trouble spots are composed of loose glacial till or man-made fill) and routing obstacles that would still be in play with shorter stations.

"While having shorter station platforms would make station-siting easier, tunnel and station depths on Ballard Link are driven primarily by the need to route around and below existing building foundations, construction tiebacks, and major utilities – not by station size," Krieg wrote in the memo. "The depth of Westlake Station, for example, is set by the need to tunnel under the foundation caissons of the Motif Hotel. These constraints exist regardless of vehicle technology or station size."

It's interesting that the agency is considering a hotel built in 1973 an immutable obstacle. Motif last sold for $145 million in February 2018 – although the 19-story tower did see a renovation in 2023, according to Puget Sound Business Journal . It's possible the agency could save more buying the property and demolishing it than routing a $20 billion-plus project around it, which would force the future Westlake Station to one of the agency's deepest ever at around 135 feet.

While on the surface Krieg's memo appeared dismissive of the idea to switching to shorter automated stations, Kubly and Reed said the agency conceded some of their key points, and framed project risk all wrong, overlooking the shortcomings of its current approach.

Kubly and Reed said they didn't consider elevated rail in their white paper because they determined it would be too large of a change to reuse the existing environmental impact statement (EIS) documentation without significant additional work. They hoped ALR would largely repurpose the existing draft EIS since it was still in a tunnel with the same tunnel locations.
The draft EIS for Ballard Link was supposed to be released this year, but has been repeatedly delayed , with foot dragging from the Trump administration likely contributing.

The delays could be an opportunity to rethink approaches, but there's no sign that's the route the agency is going. Elevated rail could offer cost savings in West Seattle, or at least expose that the agency is not reasonably estimating the cost differential between tunneling and elevating lines.

West Seattle's Junction originally was envisioned as an elevated station, but Sound Transit converted it to an underground station under the excuse that it might actually be cheaper, while reducing neighborhood opposition related to aesthetic concerns and construction detours. Shortly thereafter, the agency revealed its preferred route has ballooned in cost by $1.6 billion . Cost reductions identified in March involved dropping the Avalan Station entirely.

"There's no universe that elevating should cost more than tunneling in West Seattle based on the current land use and extensive [City-owned right-of way or ROW]. Refusing to take any of the Fauntleroy ROW is an assumption that would be contested in any objective process," Kubly and Reed told The Urbanist . "But it was a red line for the electeds/local stakeholders actually negotiating. An elevated option in downtown could be a part of the solution. We think the better approach is not to prejudge an approach, but put them in competition, through the RFI.

Across the board, the agency is largely doubling down on existing approaches to keep ST3 projects moving, even as financial headwinds grow. That approach may end up working on some lines, but advocates are worried it's failing Ballard.

The board has prioritized building out the light rail spine to Tacoma and Everett – a corridor stretching more than 60 miles. Relatedly, those project face smaller delays. Sound Transit is expecting to open Tacoma Dome Link in 2035 – three years later than first planned. The agency is hoping to launch the first leg of the Everett Link extension (as far as Paine Field) in 2037. That's only one year later than promised during the ST3 campaign. The section from Paine Field to Everett Station would wait until 2041 under the phased opening plan.
Or as Kubly opined: "Don’t be surprised to read that the results from their RFI validate their current approach."
Correction : This article was updated at 1:12pm to note that the RFI deadline has been extended by one week to October 12.

articles.title: Paid Parking Could Expand to West Seattle, Upper Queen Anne
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) has unveiled proposals that would represent the largest expansion of paid on-street parking in the city at least a decade, impacting the Alaska Junction and Upper Queen Anne business districts. The changes are intended to make it easier to access curbside parking by increasing turnover, but the idea of starting to charge for something that was previously given away for free is already proving contentious among some neighbors and business leaders.
The rollout is being paired with an expansion of dedicated vehicle loading areas, ADA accessible parking, and intersection daylighting.

SDOT's paid parking program is structured around its goal of ensuring that customers in business districts are typically able to find one or two open parking spaces on any given block. The agency calibrates parking rates with the aim of hitting its availability target range: 70% to 85% occupancy.

Twice-annual adjustments in hourly rates up or down to meet that target have been a part of life in Seattle since 2010, as part of the performance-based parking program . Those adjustment generally do not get much attention, but adding paid parking where it doesn't exist is another matter.

After conducting a field study this past April, SDOT found that 26 out of 40 blocks in West Seattle's Alaska Junction were more than 85% full, with 11 blocks out of 22 in Upper Queen Anne also clearing the bar. Several blocks in both neighborhoods were also exceeding 100% occupancy, indicating high demand was leading drivers to park in non-designated areas in ways that could impact pedestrian safety.

SDOT's proposal is to implement hourly rates from $1 to $4 per hour across approximately a dozen blocks in Alaska Junction and eight blocks in Queen Anne, along with an expansion in time-limited free parking later into the evening until 8pm. Additional time-limited load zones are also set to be put in place in both neighborhoods.

Business owners are already pushing back on SDOT's proposal, at least when it comes to Upper Queen Anne. A September 23 letter signed by an array of business leaders and residents along Queen Anne Avenue asked the department to keep on-street parking free, citing potential negative impacts that could come from adding an "additional barrier" to business access. Signees to the letter included the owners of Queen Anne Book Company, Betty Restaurant, Aluel Cellars, Bounty Kitchen, Stuhlberg's giftshop, and the director of the Queen Anne Farmer's Market.

"The businesses and organizations signing this letter are united in asking the City not to introduce paid parking on Queen Anne Avenue," the letter stated. "Free and accessible street parking is an attractive feature of the Queen Anne business district for visitors, customers, and neighborhood residents. It makes it easier to stop for a meal, run an errand, visit a local shop, attend an appointment, or spend time in the neighborhood. We are concerned that introducing paid parking would diminish that advantage and create an additional barrier to visiting local businesses."

The same letter pushed back on the idea that high occupancy rates at parking stalls in front of Queen Anne businesses do not translate to automatic support for the idea of managing that demand through pricing.

"We also want to be clear that high parking demand along Queen Anne Avenue should not be interpreted as support from the business community for paid parking," it continued. "We support improving parking availability and turnover, but paid parking is not the only tool available. Better enforcement of existing time limits, appropriately located loading zones, short- term pickup spaces, accessible parking, and adjustments to existing parking restrictions should be fully utilized before paid parking is considered."

While a paid parking program is intended to increase access to the curb allowing visitors coming by car to more easily patronize local businesses, data shows that the majority of visitors to either business district are not arriving by car at all. SDOT surveys from earlier this year found that 66% of respondents in Alaska Junction and 61% in Queen Anne arrived by walking, biking, or taking transit. This suggests that business owners could be overrepresenting the number of customers who would be deterred by having parking meters on a street.

Outside of Seattle's downtown neighborhoods, paid parking programs are relatively rare, with only a few other business districts currently requiring drivers to pay to use public curbspace. Currently just 2% of Seattle streets have parking meters at all, one main reason that a neighborhood-by-neighborhood expansion of the program is likely to be controversial, with business owners used to the way things have been operating for decades.

When it comes to Alaska Junction, paid parking has been a topic that comes up about once a decade, becoming a lightning rod every time. In both 2009 and 2018, SDOT declined to implement parking meters in the neighborhood, citing stall occupancy rates that didn't yet meet the 80% threshold. But parking demand is increasing in the neighborhood, with average parking occupancy in the 5pm hour creeping up from 75% in 2017 to 91% this year.
SDOT is accepting feedback on the parking proposals for both neighborhoods, with any changes set to be implemented in 2027.

articles.title: Health giant’s new addition to 15th Ave streetscape? Fake flowers
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Thanks to neighbor Tammy Jo for the picture
Hopefully these new Capitol Hill flowers are not permanent-e .

Neighbors in the CHS Facebook Group have made note of a chintzy new addition to Kaiser Permanente’s Capitol Hill campus just as the health giant is about to embark on $2.5 million in clinical upgrades to its 15th Ave facilities.
“Kaiser on 15th has filled their planters with plastic flowers,” Tim notes . “Not at all tacky.”
Others agreed this may be a case where phony flowers are not better than nothing.

Whether any hospital officials are appreciating the sarcasm is not known. CHS is trying to sort out who at the California-based integrated managed care consortium to contact about the new landscaping.

The strange cost-saving measure comes as Kaiser is preparing major renovations within the main 15th and Thomas hospital complex including a $2.12 million Level 1 overhaul and supply conversions following its announcement that it would hold off on ER billing changes and add 25 inpatient beds, increasing capacity from 18 to 43 across intensive care, telemetry, and medical–surgical units.

Kaiser Permanente’s relationship with the surrounding neighborhood could also use some care. The health provider has been touting efforts to fill its street-fronting spaces with new businesses but the spaces have remained empty over recent years. Meanwhile, its complex surface parking lots remain underutilized neighborhood spaces .
A more than $400 million planned campus overhaul still on the books following Kaiser’s 2017 acquisition of Group Health has also, apparently, been downsized.

articles.title: ‘Abandoned by the city’ — Letter calls for more maintenance and outreach resources as disorder at Cal Anderson Park causes ‘trickle-down effect’
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The sports field turf was quickly repaired this summer. Next summer will bring a $2.8 million full overhaul of the field

A group of Capitol Hill business leaders, residents, and the Cal Anderson Park Alliance sent a joint letter to Mayor Katie Wilson , the Seattle City Council , and Seattle Parks and Recreation calling for new solutions following a summer marked by deteriorating conditions and escalating safety concerns.

The letter, co-signed by the GSBA chamber of commerce, property developers Hunters Capital and Dunn & Hobbes , and neighborhood advocates, argues that neglect has created an environment of public safety risk that spills directly onto Broadway and the Pike/Pine commercial corridor.

“Cal Anderson desperately needs increased investment in the stewardship and beauty of the park. A visitor to the area during Pride weekend would have seen a park full of trampled, yellow grass and dying flowers, an empty wading pool filled with the remains of a bonfire, tire treads along park pathways, litter, and more,” the letter reads. “The area looks less like a reflection of the community’s character and more like a grassy hill with a water feature.”
“Neglected stewardship lends credence to the perception that Cal Anderson has been abandoned by the city,” the letter reads.
Public safety breakdowns over the peak summer months served as the primary catalyst for the coalition’s appeal.

The people behind the letter said that unchecked drug activity along Nagle Place and restroom overdoses in neighboring shops have dissuaded visitors, culminating in holiday disorder on Bobby Morris Field . “Fireworks activity that occurred in Cal Anderson over the Fourth of July weekend presents a microcosm of these issues at play,” the letter stated, citing an incident where a large group of people burned e-bikes and scooters in a bonfire while fire crews waited for police to intervene.

Cal Anderson’s basketball court was also the scene of a reported accidental shooting in August that sent a man to the hospital while the Seattle Police Department said it began conducting extra patrols near the park after neighbor complaints about noise and drugs.
The city’s new budget proposal includes funding for Cal Anderson’s restrooms

The letter asks that the city convene an inter-departmental task force, fund consistent place-based outreach for the park’s unhoused population, and boost patrols by Park Rangers , the CARE department, and Seattle Police.

Neither Mayor Katie Wilson nor Seattle City Council President Joy Hollingsworth have made a public response to the letter and neither office responded to a request for details of any plans for addressing the complaints.

However, local mutual-aid group The Stone Soup Crew released a counter-response, agreeing on the necessity of park investment but urging City Hall to empower unhoused park regulars as paid stewards rather than increasing police enforcement.

The Salvation Army outreach effort Street Level currently holds a $1.2 million contract for outreach in the area covering all of Capitol Hill and the Central District. The letter claims the organization has only two employees to cover the entirety of the District 3 assignment.

The city’s current 2027-2028 budget process could provide resources for addressing some of the issues. Though there has been no discussion of Cal Anderson-specific amendments to date, the current proposal includes expanded funding for parks rangers, park restroom renovations and maintenance, $714,000 for parks buskers and increases in general park maintenance programs, and maintaining funding for place-based community safety and commercial corridor activations that include Capitol Hill. An additional $75,000 has been earmarked specifically for public space activation and community-led events on Capitol Hill parks primarily focused on Cal Anderson and $25,000 for art murals, lighting, and graffiti deterrence at the Cal Anderson restroom structure aimed at reducing vandalism and preventing drug usage in and around park facilities.

articles.title: Dick’s Drive-In settles worker lawsuit, blasts state’s surge in class actions
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Puget Sound burger chain Dick’s Drive-In announced it has reached a settlement in a proposed class-action wage-and-hour lawsuit, according to an update sent to customers.

The lawsuit filed early this year by California-based Justice Law Corporation on behalf of a former employee, alleged the restaurant chain failed to provide required 10-minute rest breaks and 30-minute meal periods mandated under Washington state labor law.
The potential class-action lawsuit could have involved hundreds of employees including workers at the chain’s Broadway location.

While the agreement awaits final approval in King County Superior Court , Dick’s leadership denies any wrongdoing, maintaining they have documented proof of accurate pay and proper breaks. Executives stated the settlement was a practical business decision to avoid the crippling expense and distraction of multi-year litigation.

In the statement, Dick’s criticized Washington’s regulatory climate and the surge in employment class actions, noting plaintiff attorneys will collect over $600,000 from the deal. Management urged eligible current and former workers to accept their settlement payouts.

The company’s Broadway drive-in is one of the most popular fast food stops on Capitol Hill. This summer, new paperwork was filed for early permitting work for a possible new Capitol Hill McDonald’s only a block away but there have been no new filings for the possible big chain Dick’s competition since.

articles.title: Rainier Beach Businesses Address Safety While Helping Their Shops Thrive
paras: A cluster of shops flank Rainier Avenue South near Seward Park Avenue, an intersection that usually hums with a steady stream of cars. The area is a business anchor among South Seattle, Renton, and Skyway, offering food, a salon, a fitness space, and auto-repair services.

"The neighborhood has seen notable recent changes. Ashanti Mayfield's Creamy Cone Cafe , which served up ice cream scoops for five years, closed abruptly in August. Creamy Cone is still taking orders for catering events and pop-ups. Several blocks away to the west, near Safeway, a brick-and-mortar Starbucks closed in September after having set up shop last fall.
When the business owners talk about the neighborhood they're rooted in, safety, transportation, and community are common themes.

Ten years ago, Harold Fields started selling his okazupan — fried breads stuffed with savory fillings, such as BBQ pork, chicken curry, and other flavors — from the Umami Kushi storefront. He sells his breads to Uwajimaya and other shops around the region, but he wants South End neighbors to visit his shop too. "There's no [transit] access for anyone outside the South End to get to you unless they're in a car," said Fields.

"He blames this on a lack of resources and attention to transportation in the region. He said the neighborhood doesn't have an anchor institution, like a hospital or university, that brings in commuters — an institution that could drive investment in infrastructure. Fields mentioned there are also no real transit connections to the Rainier Beach light rail station on Martin Luther King Way South and South Henderson Street, and bus service is infrequent.

Fields criticized closing down Lake Washington Park Boulevard to cars this summer without offering other options for southward travel. "They closed a major arterial route on the South End, but haven't added any extra bus routes or options. People still have to get to work." Fields has proposed a public transportation loop to the City and County that connects the light rail station to the Rainier Beach neighborhood business area, Be'er Sheva Park, Pritchard Island Beach, and Kubota Garden. Fields is opening a second Umami Kushi shop in the former Molly Moon's walk-up shop in Madrona.

Daoud Abouchamsddin brought Paranormal Pie to the neighborhood in 2017 and runs it with his nephew, Nael Said. The family has run Lebanese and Mediterranean restaurants around the region for decades. All of the offerings on Paranormal Pie's menu are halal, so pizzas feature beef pepperoni and turkey ham. They also serve up pasta, sandwiches, hummus, dolmathes, and baklava.

Said recounted being told by people outside of the community that Rainier Beach is dangerous, but when he and his wife passed out flyers in the neighborhood to announce the restaurant opening, he was moved by how well the neighbors knew each other. "The people here are super friendly and welcoming," he said. "We never worried about safety until the last few years, when there have been more shootings." Looking out the large front windows, Said mentioned that traffic on Rainier Avenue South is fast and busy. "Slower-paced traffic and walking-friendly [streets] would bring more pedestrians."
As Jack Chung stood in front of Seward Park Market and Deli, customers walked in, often greeting him with "Hi, Uncle Jack." Chung set up the shop 12 years ago. His son, Richard, owns it now.

In addition to convenience-store fare, they have fried chicken and other hot snacks. It's a business Jack Chung knows well since he's operated convenience stores for four decades. He says it's a good neighborhood, close to downtown and the airport. He lives nearby too. He admitted there are shootings but said shootings happen throughout the city. "[With business,] it's simple: If you know people, no problem with business. They'll listen to you if you know them."

Sophia Ellis sat in a chair on the sidewalk in front of her market that sells Caribbean seasonings, condiments, and provisions. She chatted with neighbors and watched the street. Ellis brought this business to the neighborhood four years ago. This shop is the merging of a Caribbean market she owned on Martin Luther King Jr. Way South and a food truck she ran in Skyway for seven years. She cooks jerk chicken, oxtail, and curry goat at the back of the shop.

Ellis feeds many people. She offered food to youth through the program All Youth Can Eat during September, and she will feed hungry children anytime when they stop by the shop. She also delivers food to unhoused people. Ellis, who grew up in Portmore, Jamaica, says her work and values come from her family. "My granddad had a shop where he sold food and groceries. My grandmother was like this, cooked for everybody. Sunday, she'd cook, and everybody comes and everybody's eating."

The store recently experienced its seventh break-in in a year. "It's the same person each time," said Ellis. "The police wouldn't come to the site, and would only take a statement over the phone two hours later."

Van Tieu opened Van Go Auto Glass in 2020. His business replaces all types of auto glass, including sunroofs, and they tint windows and restore headlights. They also travel to customers who can't drive because of windshield damage.

Tieu's father started Dan's Auto Repair across the street in the 1990s and retired a number of years ago. "On the weekends, we'd come [to his shop] and help my dad to be with the family," said Tieu. Tieu's brother, John, operates Dan's Auto Repair.

Planted along the side of the auto glass shop are a few dozen fig trees. "I like to garden and have some green space at the shop,” said Tieu. He said he has over a hundred fig varieties at his home in Skyway.

Tieu has also experienced a number of break-ins over the years. "It can be a rough corner. There are shootings too, but we try to prevent it by [the stores] being close-knit and [watching] for each other," said Tieu. "Overall, the area is safer than 30 years ago. Now you see more people wanting to live in the neighborhood, more businesses than before." He also noted that parking has become an issue for some residents because of new developments built with little or no parking.

Kim Lam has been the manager at Crawfish & Hot Pot Seafood House for more than two years. After the Crawfish Boil owners left, Truc Nguyen and Binh Lam took over the business. They kept the Louisiana seafood boil and added pho and rice dishes to the menu.

Lam grew up in the Othello neighborhood. "I love how everything is in walking distance," said Lam about the South End. "When my mom was busy with work, I would get a banh mi and go to Othello Park with my brother and friends to hang out." She said the restaurant is supported by regulars in the area and people who drive in from as far as Bellevue, Lynnwood, and Olympia for the dishes. Lam loves Rainier Beach and the community created in the restaurant. The biggest concern for Lam is the shootings. About 12 shots were fired near the store in July.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, October 5–11
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Nathalie Graham, Amanda Manitach, and Dave Segal
paras: (COMMUNITY) The annual Week Without Driving kicked off on October 1 and runs through October 8. Are you participating? Even if you haven’t yet, it’s not too late. It’s a fun challenge: Can you get around your city without a car? You’ll have to rely on the bus, a bike, or your own two feet. How long can you go? It’s a good way to appreciate the services at our fingertips, especially with Seattle Prop. 1 on the ballot next month. That proposition will raise sale tax to renew and expand the Seattle Transit Measure that funds our bus service. You better vote yes. Week Without Driving will show you why. If you’re looking for a specific Week Without Driving event, check out the Nondrivers Alliance’s event with law professor Michael Pollack , the author of Sidewalk Nation: The Life and Law of America’s Most Overlooked Resource , on October 5 at the Husky Union Building on University of Washington’s campus. ( Husky Union Building, 6:30–8 pm, free with RSVP ) NATHALIE GRAHAM

(VISUAL ART) It’s fitting that Surge, an exhibition that pairs visual artists with scientists to make work about climate change, takes place at the Museum of Northwest Art, located in La Conner, Washington. Climate change isn’t just a hypothetical in the Skagit basin, a 3,115-square-mile watershed that extends from the Cascades to the Skagit Bay. It’s experienced firsthand as the sea spills over levees, roads go underwater, and the familiar ways of doing things are swept away. This is the fourth iteration of Surge, curated by Chloé Dye Sherpe, and it’s always fascinating to see what happens when artists spend quality time in the trenches with the climatologists, hydrologists, biologists, and governmental policymakers tracking the changes that directly affect our region. This year’s robust roster includes artists working across media, from neon and glass to painting and assemblage: Holly Ballard Martz, Kelsey Fernkopf and Steve Gilbert, Melinda Hurst Frye, Morgan Madison, Steve Jensen, Sue Danielson, and Niki Keenan, to name but a few. ( Museum of Northwest Art ) AMANDA MANITACH

(FILM) John Wilson is a documentarian of the absurd. On his endlessly fascinating HBO comedy docuseries How To with John Wilson , he delves deep into themes as far-reaching as the Mandela effect, scaffolding, and circumcision, pasting together disparate clips of footage into a kind of collage to hilarious effect as he narrates via voiceover. His investigations end up leading him to the most unexpected places and put the dizzying spectrum of humanity on full display. That’s why I’m so excited for his new film, The History of Concrete , in which he attempts to apply a formula for writing and selling a hit Hallmark-style movie to a documentary about, yes, concrete. If anyone can make this topic riveting, it’s him, and I’m willing to bet you’ll never look at a sidewalk the same way again. ( SIFF Cinema Uptown & Tasveer Film Center, times vary ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) America’s most uncompromising hip-hop group, New Jersey’s Dälek, have been enlightening and blowing minds since 1998. A staunch advocate for POC’s rights, MC Dälek (aka Will Brooks) trenchantly rails against oppression and strife, from now to centuries back, with an authoritative bellow and a conspiratorial sneer while he and producer/instrumentalist Mike Manteca fuse industrial noise, drone, and funk into towers of sonic power. Their newest album, 2026’s Brilliance of a Falling Moon , takes a flamethrower to the fa$cist ruling class. This decade’s awful times have motivated Dälek to rise to even higher heights of lyrical causticity and sonic brutality. After 28 years of public service in the underground-hip-hop trenches, they’ve proved themselves to be the true heirs to Public Enemy’s crown. ( Funhouse, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL

(BOOKS) Last year, Top Chef fan favorite and lesbian heartthrob Melissa King released her James Beard Award-winning debut cookbook Cook Like a King . You may recall that she and the show’s host Padma Lakshmi sent the collective sapphic universe into a gay panic with their flirty Instagram banter while simultaneously promoting their books, plus there was a sultry Gomez and Morticia couple costume that ignited dating rumors. (They’re just friends, or so they claim…) Now, King is back with her memoir The Girl Who Became King . The book shares her story of growing up queer in a Shanghainese and Cantonese family in Los Angeles’s Gabriel Valley, her initiation into the high-stakes world of Michelin-starred restaurants, and her Top Chef journey. She’ll share her story with food writer, photographer, designer, and Little Fat Boy blogger Frankie Gaw at this event, hosted by Charlie’s Queer Books at Ballard Homestead. ( Ballard Homestead, 7 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(PARTY) Everyone knows that Halloween is gay Christmas, and this party at Asylum Collective for “lesbians, bisexuals, femmes, butches, trans girls, nonbinary babes, sapphics, spooky little freaks + the people who love themmmmm” is the perfect opportunity to celebrate. You can look forward to DJs, dancing, free candy, tarot reading, and tattoos. Costumes are strongly encouraged and there will be contests for the best dressed—channel your inner Carmilla by dressing up as a hot lesbian vampiress and dance your ass off to “Red Wine Supernova.” ( Asylum Collective, 9 pm–1 am, 21+ ) JULIANNE BELL
The Blair Witch Project: Film Screening and Q&A

(FILM) Even if you’re not a horror fan, you undoubtedly know The Blair Witch Project , thanks to its prescient marketing hoax campaign, which leveraged the early internet to blur the boundaries of fact and fiction. The 1999 low-budget sleeper hit, which was primarily shot over the course of eight days, takes the form of a found-footage pseudo-documentary and famously listed its actors as “deceased” or “missing.” It’s not just a stunt, though: The film is genuinely haunting and understands that the unseen is more terrifying than the most gruesome monster special effects could ever conjure. This special screening at the 5th Avenue Theatre is an opportunity to see it in all its unsettling glory on the big screen, followed by a Q&A session with original cast members Heather Donahue, Joshua Leonard, and Michael C. Williams (all three alive and well). ( 5th Avenue Theatre, 7:30 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

articles.title: Slog AM: Katie Wilson Is Impatient With Herself, Brazil Presidential Election Heads to Runoff, Orcs Protest Palantir
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: I am a global citizen. Just read my wedding diary . Maybe that’s why the news out of Brazil (where I started my career ) and Morocco (where much of my family is from) caught my eye this morning. Don’t worry, I’m also keeping an eye on Seattle City Hall’s budget haggling.

Katie Wilson “is as impatient as everyone else” about her slow pace of reform, including dismantling homeless encampments and enacting progressive taxation. Wilson sat down with Seattle Nice and acknowledged how she’s continuing the practice of dismantling homeless encampments without offering shelter to people evicted (aka, sweeps); the punitive pushing around of her predecessors. She stressed the importance of creating good “vibes” for the business community, and made some nuanced arguments about the role of the Seattle Police Department and Law Enforcement Assisted Diversion in arresting and referring our way out of the public drug market crisis ( worth a listen! ).

Sheriffs across WA shall remain unaccountable to Olympia: On Friday, Thurston County Superior Court Judge Christine Schaller blocked key elements of a law passed by the Legislature this year that set standards for sheriffs, a role that is usually elected, that required them to have five years of law enforcement experience and no serious convictions, to be at least 25 years old, and to undergo background checks. It also allowed for their removal from office. Schaller’s ruling is the latest blow to accountability for sheriffs from the courts.

Alleged Chinese spy arrested, faces charges related to surveilling Taiwanese official’s family in Seattle: KING5 reports that the woman allegedly rented a car in Seattle, drove to the person’s house, and photographed the family and their vehicle, according to US officials. The images were sent to a Chinese official on WeChat.

The first union on Capitol Hill: California Rep . Ro Khanna’s staff have unionized, Politico reports . It’s the first time workers in the US legislature have done so. And it only took four years after a union vote in the Democrat’s office to actually get it done.

Brazil’s elections keep rhyming with America’s. Every four years, the world watches in horror as Americans go to the polls in embarrassingly low numbers to determine how the US will meddle with or support their futures. We experience a tiny fragment of this. In Brazil, elections predict how much of the Amazon Rainforest will get cut down. I was glued to the Rio Times coverage of Brazil’s runoff election results for the past 24 hours. Incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has reduced deforestation significantly, CarbonBrief calculates. His former rival, Trump fan Jair Bolsonaro, led a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, got convicted, and is currently in jail . The election was between Lula and Bolsonaro’s son.

Bolsonaro’s son got more votes: Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, has been running in his father’s place to carry the torch in a political alliance that is pro-gun, pro-Bible, all-in on agriculture (including slash and burn operations in the Amazon). Flávio Bolsonaro won 47 percent of the recent election vs. Lula’s 45 percent. Since neither won a majority, there will be a runoff. Lula is a center-left leader way past his prime (he’s 80) who helped bring a generation of Brazilians out of poverty. He’s too damn old to inspire the left and, like Biden, didn’t trust anyone to pass the torch to on his admittedly shallow bench. Brazilian voters go back to the polls on Oct. 25 to decide between Bolsonaro Jr. and Lula.

Death-from-the-sky maker Shield AI is expanding in Seattle , GeekWire reports .One priority of Mayor Katie Wilson’s is to diversify the economy amid a potential slide in tech. Well, there’s always the defense industrial complex. Shield AI makes the X-BAT, an “AI-piloted strike fighter” that outranges a Lockheed Martin F-35A and drops 2,000-pound bombs ( like the ones used on Gaza ). It’s planning to expand production to a warehouse near SeaTac.

Meanwhile, out of work “orcs” tried to get work at Palantir’s Seattle office. The LOTR-inspired company is involved in ICE’s surveillance of protesters , and gets a lot of Army contracts . It’s the latest milquetoast protest from Climate Defiance:

Morocco’s first female Prime Minister enjoyed her first weekend in power, blessed by the patriarchy. The New York Times notes that King Mohammed VI appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as the third female head of state in a North African country. At the same time, the NYT suggests Moroccan women generally aren’t advancing as quickly in society as their representatives. We’ll see if Moroccan feminism and empowerment can filter down.

Morocco is America’s oldest ally, in a way: It was the first to recognize US independence in 1777 . Back then, we asked (paid) them to let up on the piracy and they agreed. Lately, our deals have been about expanding colonialism. Morocco has agreed to recognize the State of Israel , in exchange for the US recognizing Morocco’s sovereignty over Western Sahara, whose people are only tied to Morocco because of Spanish colonization and dictatorship. You may have seen some of the region if you watched The Odyssey .

Seattle-area ferries delayed or cancelled due to lack of crew: KOMO reports that many routes are down to one boat or out of service entirely. Check the latest WSDOT delays ; this morning there were a lot of cancelled Bremerton/Seattle boats.

paras: The vice-president’s recent remarks seek to maintain a posture of strength while they inadvertently expose political realities

JD Vance has parachuted into the midterm election campaign on a rescue mission in a new guise: a risk management consultant. Speaking in the flat language of the expert hired to identify threats, weaknesses and losses affecting a business’s reputation, he has presented his executive summary for limiting vulnerabilities and a scenario for averting disaster.

“There’s a lot of good that’s been done, but there’s a lot of work left to do,” he informed his clients on 15 September about the words to use. “Give us another chance, or give us another couple of years, to continue to work on the amazing things that we’ve been doing for the past two years.” He turned the focus to harm reduction rather than total agreement and then shifted the equation to a negative binary choice. “Even if you don’t agree with us on every issue, the other party is consumed by craziness.”

Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man , Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth . articles.title: My sister Nicole married OJ Simpson. This is what I wish I had known

paras: Since Nicole Brown Simpson’s murder in 1994, Denise Brown has devoted herself to ending domestic violence. She talks about her beloved sister, the trauma she witnessed in the couple’s marriage and how lives can be saved

The last night Denise Brown spent with her sister Nicole Brown Simpson was at a restaurant for a family celebration. Nicole looked out of the window. “All of a sudden she goes, ‘Oh my God, there he is.’ He was driving by.” Brown looked out, trying to get a glimpse of her sister’s ex-husband, the former American football star OJ Simpson. “I saw these headlights. She said, ‘He’s constantly following me.’” They went back to talking about their plans for the summer.

The following morning, 13 June 1994, Brown was up early at her parents’ house in Orange County in southern California, when the phone rang shortly after 6am. “I heard my mom scream a scream that I had never heard from a human being,” says Brown. “It was so guttural. Just awful.”

articles.title: Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual | Steven Greenhouse

articles.title: Metallica review – metal titans on fine form in spectacular rarities-focused show
articles.author: Sam Hockley-Smith
paras: Sphere, Las Vegas The first night of a new residency is an immersive plunge into the band’s visual world that showcases the depth of their catalog

Las Vegas’s Sphere takes on the characteristics of whatever it’s advertising on its exterior. Depending on when you look, you might see Orbi, the Sphere mascot, winking at you, or an ad for one of their Wizard of Oz showings, or maybe a roiling mass of red flames and shocks of lightning announcing the arrival of Metallica for their residency Life Burns Faster. Looking at it feels like staring at the end times. It’s like a huge black hole, sucking in the jittery sun-blasted energy of Vegas and transmuting it into an ominous ode to the renegade titans of thrash, but, you know, an older, wiser, therapized version of the band.

This is the first night of Metallica’s 24-show residency, and it features the return of their “no repeat” format, meaning they play twice a week without repeating a single song during that week. It’s a showcase of the breadth of their catalogue as much as it’s a reminder of just how many indelible classics they’ve written. It also makes for a more interesting show. It’s not especially difficult for Metallica to play hours of hits, but it’s more fun when they forgo a few obvious ones in favor of a larger narrative.

articles.title: US migrant flights to Liberia evoke troubling history of sending people deemed unwanted to the West African nation
articles.author:
<name>Karen Masterson, Assistant Professor of Journalism, University of Richmond</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/karen-masterson-2768317"/>
paras: The Supreme Court’s recent decision to temporarily allow the United States to resume deporting migrants to third-country destinations could see the resumption of flights to Liberia.

About the size of Ohio, the West African country is one of 35 countries the Trump administration is paying to shelter and feed Latin Americans and others living in the U.S. without proper legal status. Some of those receiving nations have a reputation for corruption and human rights abuses , and in most cases, those being deported have no links to the host nation.
The policy may ultimately be deemed unconstitutional, but on Sept. 29, 2026, the Supreme Court justices gave the green light for flights to continue while they consider the policy’s legality.
So far, at least 20 U.S. deportees have been flown to Liberia. One Colombian national who arrived in the African nation on Aug. 20 told PBS : “Honestly, I had never heard of Liberia.”

While those being deported to Liberia may not be familiar with the country, the same can’t be said for American policymakers. Unlike the other countries participating in the Trump administration’s efforts, Liberia has a long history with American immigration policy.

As a scholar who has written about that history , I see echoes of past U.S. efforts to move nonwhite people to Liberia in the latest removals. Indeed, it is those past events that gave Liberia its name.
In the early 1800s, Africa’s west coast attracted American leaders who were looking for a place to send those they viewed as unwanted U.S. residents: free people of African descent.

The region became the endpoint for America’s first massive removal campaign, starting in 1820, focused on relocating Black people “ back to Africa .” The chief U.S. organization advocating for this effort was the American Colonization Society , created in 1816.

The initial wave of departures was made up of African American intellectuals, church leaders and merchants. The brutality and inhumanity that white Americans inflicted on free and enslaved Black people drove them out. Many abolitionists and Quakers – who fought to ban slavery – initially supported the colonization society’s removal efforts as a means for helping Black residents escape the cruelty of American laws, especially the Fugitive Slave Acts .

But the true driving force was the slaveholder class, which held a majority in Congress. Those politicians demanded the deportations because they knew the presence of free Black people gave hope to the millions in bondage — who, in some states, outnumbered white people.

These early American settlers named their new home Liberia, for liberty. And by 1847, they fought the colonization society’s control over the land and turned the settlement into the first independent republic in Africa . They set up towns and farms along the coastline, which had local indigenous communities estimated to be in the hundreds of thousands .

By the end of the century, some 16,000 Black Americans made the journey, many against their will and all on the promise of a better life. Thousands more joined them, some from the Caribbean and at least 6,000 who were rescued from slave-trading vessels, intercepted and sent to Liberia by the U.S. Navy.

The colonization society’s mass deportation plan was a nationwide effort with powerful political leaders and slaveholders like Henry Clay , who was a U.S. senator, speaker of the House, secretary of state and three-time presidential candidate; Francis Scott Key , a famous U.S. attorney best known for writing “The Star Spangled Banner”; and Bushrod Washington , a Supreme Court justice and nephew of George Washington.

Ten Southern state legislatures endorsed the idea by passing laws that allowed the freeing of an enslaved person only when deportation out of the state was arranged and paid for. The colonization society raised the funds to pay for their removal to Liberia.

Some abolitionists and future leaders, including Abraham Lincoln , at first supported colonization because they believed it would help accelerate emancipation. But over time, and especially during the Civil War, most instead supported citizen rights for Black residents.

The effort was also opposed by powerful public intellectuals, including Frederick Douglass, who helped convince many — including Lincoln — of the need to secure freedom and justice for Black people in a country where they already lived.
At least 20% of those who made the journey to Liberia in the 1800s died of malaria. The rest dealt with supply shortages, severe weather, failed crops and hostility from indigenous communities.
But most white Americans knew none of this . They were told Liberia had fertile soil and a healthy climate; it was a promised land for Black people wishing to go home.

Harriet Beecher Stowe, in her best-selling novel “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” furthered this notion by having her main characters, on a hair-raising and violent odyssey to escape enslavement, finally find freedom and peace on a boat headed to Liberia .

Douglass praised her novel in his newspaper, but for this last part of it, which he vehemently opposed . Douglass wrote to Stowe : “We are here, and here we are likely to remain. … We have grown up with this Republic; and I see nothing in our character … which compels the belief that we must leave the United States.”

The American Colonization Society’s strong influence on deportations ended with the Civil War, though the organization continued raising money and influencing U.S. policy until it was dissolved in 1964.

Other independent waves of migration to Liberia followed, especially as the end of Reconstruction unleashed white-led terrorism against Black communities throughout the South. This included the Liberian Exodus Joint Stock Steamship Company, a Black-owned business that transported well-off African Americans to Liberia in 1878. Its schooner carried some of Liberia’s soon-to-be-famous families from Charleston, South Carolina, to Liberia’s capital, Monrovia.

In my view, what they accomplished along West Africa’s windward coast is astounding and, unfortunately, forgotten by most Americans. I’ve collected thousands of records from archives, including the U.S. National Archives, that show how surviving “Americo-Liberians,” as they called themselves, used grit and ingenuity to build large farming operations, grow merchant fleets, establish fisheries and spur other industries in their efforts to be integrated into Western global markets.

Yet for all the successes in difficult circumstances, Liberia in the 20th century remained in America’s shadow. After decades of fending off European attempts to absorb it into their colonial holdings , Liberia sought refuge in its historical relationship with the U.S. And in the 1920s, the two countries began a “ special friendship .” At a time when Jim Crow laws ravaged the American South, U.S. business interests created a plantation economy in Liberia rooted in resource extraction that enriched large U.S. companies, including Firestone Tire and Republic Steel .

Archival records show the corruption that grew from deals benefiting the few at the expense of the many that became a long-term driver in the country’s political instability, resulting in civil strife and poverty that has wracked the country for decades.

For many of the 1,200 people earmarked for deportation to Liberia in the coming months by the U.S. government, landing in the capital, Monrovia, may feel cruel. That it was once a thriving city of Black elites whose forebearers arrived there from America may feel meaningless.

The circumstances of their deportations to Liberia are obviously very different form earlier waves. Those being deported today weren’t captured and sold into bondage; many left home to escape civil war, gang violence or starvation.

But there is a common driver between American policymakers now and those in the 19th century in encouraging and enforcing deportation to Liberia: a desire to rid the U.S. of nonwhite people deemed to represent a problem at home.
In December 2026, the Supreme Court will hear arguments and ultimately decide the constitutionality of this desire, as written into today’s rapid deportation policies.
