articles.title: Fewer Americans are getting help buying groceries from SNAP benefits as states grapple with the program’s cascade of changes
articles.author:
<name>Tracy Roof, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Richmond</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/tracy-roof-911241"/>
paras: The number of people enrolled in the Supplemental Nutritional Assistance Program is falling fast. The program formerly known as food stamps helped roughly 42 million Americans put food on the table in 2025.

As of June 2026, the most recent data available, the number of people enrolled in the program in the whole country had declined by almost 13% to 36.4 million . Among those no longer getting benefits are an estimated 1.5 million children .
President Donald Trump says a strong economy has driven down demand for the program.

It’s possible that some people have left the program because their incomes rose. But the enrollment decline has a lot to do with the big tax-and-spending package the president signed into law in July 2025 .
For example, the law caused some immigrants residing legally in the country, such as refugees and those seeking asylum, to no longer be eligible for SNAP benefits.

In addition, more people enrolled in SNAP now may only get up to three months of benefits if they don’t work, engage in training programs or volunteer at least 80 hours a month. These work requirements previously applied only to adults up to the age of 54; that cutoff is rising to 64. Another change is that parents of older children ages 14-17 are now expected to meet these work requirements .

All states are phasing in these restrictions, but the number of people getting SNAP benefits is falling much faster in some states than others. That includes Arizona, where enrollment has fallen by almost half , along with Louisiana and Illinois , where it’s down by about one-fifth.
And now, states must pay more to run SNAP , which is federally funded but state-administered.

In my research on the history of SNAP, I’ve found that changes in the way states run their programs have a big impact on who can get help. States are struggling to adapt to new federal policies. As additional changes roll out, more families may lose access to SNAP.

As of Oct. 1, 2026, states have to pay 75% of all administrative costs, which include paying staff who manage the enrollment process and maintaining the program’s computer systems. Previously, states paid 50% of those costs. The federal government estimates that states and local governments will pay roughly US$17 billion more in administrative costs over the next five years.

In the 2027 fiscal year, which began on Oct. 1, California – with the largest population of any state – will be responsible for paying roughly $670 million more to run the program. Wyoming, with the smallest number of residents, will pay about $3 million more .
Costs will be shifted to local governments in nine of the 10 states where SNAP is administered by counties.

State agencies and some state legislatures are imposing stricter rules and requiring applicants to provide more paperwork documenting their income, expenses and the number of people in their household.
Caseworkers in states such as Arizona have reportedly been overwhelmed with the paperwork. Those seeking help have spent hours trying to get through on phone lines and have faced monthslong delays.

States are taking these steps to get ready for another change that will roll out in October 2027. At that point, many states will also have to cover up to 15% of the costs of benefits for the first time since the program began in the 1960s.
This cost is much larger than the administrative costs and could be staggering for many states .

How much a state pays will be based on its “payment error rate.” These error rates measure how much in benefits are paid above or below what families are actually entitled to based on their household size, income and expenses. It is calculated based on an in-depth review of a small sample of a state’s benefits payments each year.

These inaccurate payments are generally a result of mistakes on the part of the applicant or their caseworker – they rarely are the result of fraud. The payment error rate includes benefits paid to ineligible participants. It does not include payments never made to applicants who were eligible for benefits but wrongly denied them or incorrectly dropped from the program.
Supporters of SNAP argue that this makes states err on the side of denying benefits.
States with an error rate less than 6% won’t face new costs for benefits. But only nine states had rates that low in 2025.

States with an error rate between 6% and 8% will be responsible for 5% of the costs of their residents’ SNAP benefits. States with an error rate between 8% and 10% will have to cover 10%. States with error rates over 10% will have to cover 15%.

There’s a weird twist: If a state has an error rate over 13.32% , it won’t have to pay part of the cost of residents’ SNAP benefits for up to two years as they would have had it been in the 6% to 13.32% range.

To reduce their error rates, states need to invest in more staff, training, technology and better application and verification procedures. But states had little time to do all that. The states’ share of costs slated to kick in as of October 2027 is based on the error rates in the fiscal year that ended in September 2026.
Organizations representing state and local governments and social workers are pushing for an across-the board two-year delay.

What’s more, legislation known as the “ farm bill ,” which sets policies for agriculture, conservation and food-related assistance like SNAP, is now ensnared in the dispute. Democrats, whose support is needed to pass the legislation in the Senate, would like to see most of the new SNAP changes repealed.
Congress aims to pass a farm bill roughly every five years, but the most recent one, which was finalized in 2018, has expired .

Short of rolling back all the SNAP policy changes, many Democrats have refused to vote for the farm bill unless it includes a two-year delay for all states in shouldering part of the cost of SNAP benefits.
If the Democratic Party holds a majority in one or both chambers of Congress after the 2026 midterm elections, their leverage could increase in these negotiations.

The Republican Party’s version of the farm bill now pending in the Senate includes a one-year delay in the benefits-funding changes. But it would increase the states’ burden even more than the policy planned for October 2027. That’s a nonstarter for Democrats.

Meanwhile, there are many signs that a large share of the people who have lost their SNAP benefits are struggling to feed their families. More people, for example, are seeking help from food pantries and banks , which fear they will not be able to keep up with growing demand.
It’s hard to predict what might happen next.
SNAP’s higher costs could force states and counties to raise taxes, cut spending on other programs or find ways to reduce spending on SNAP.
Officials in some states are saying that they may find they need to drop the program altogether .

Because states lack the authority to change benefit amounts or do much to directly limit who qualifies for the program, I believe more states will be tempted to add red tape to lower their error rates, reduce the number of people getting benefits, or both.

Tracy Roof does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
articles.author:
<name>Raghupathy Sivakumar, Vice President of Commercialization and Chief Commercialization Officer, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/raghupathy-sivakumar-2767284"/>
paras: Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their unemployment rate hit 5.7% , compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s one of the worst rates in the past 20 years.
Meanwhile, roughly 4 in 10 graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic.

As an educator for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate?

What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok attained that threshold in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly.

Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers.

I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit.

The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences develop the capabilities students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers.
Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech.

Making adaptability a core skill: Students need to learn how to be nimble . This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world.

To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator .
The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape.

Understanding customer value: Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech .

Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level.

Emphasizing fundamentals: Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate.
Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value.

But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course.

That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback.

More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, such as Cornell and the University of Washington . At Georgia Tech, we have a playbook that we have developed through our experiences that follows the following principles:

Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum: One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out.

Build a pathway to business creation: Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, including MIT , Rice University and the University of Texas .

But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a learn/make/launch/scale pathway that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them.

Offer real venture experience: A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch. After all, since most startups tend to fail , confidence is a value that successful entrepreneurs have to sustain.

There’s another important element that’s needed: private sector partnerships. Fortunately, entrepreneurial education is well aligned with the interests of universities’ traditional corporate partners.

These companies, especially those with established, successful business models, are eager to hire students with a strong understanding of fundamentals and entrepreneurial confidence. This next generation can help the companies navigate the future.

Companies can also offer industry know-how, mentorship opportunities and financial and in-kind support. And they understand that students building a startup have to think beyond their own discipline to succeed. For example, an engineering student will need to understand customers, pricing, finance, sales, operations, intellectual property and team building. That broader perspective can make them more effective when they enter a corporate environment full time.

The same capabilities can also translate into venture creation itself: The value of entrepreneurial education can be seen across both traditional workforce pathways and startup outcomes. Our experience at Georgia Tech offers evidence of both.

Startups launched by Georgia Tech students over the past decade have crossed US$4.5 billion in aggregate total valuation and have created thousands of jobs. We’ve also found encouraging early evidence that students who gain confidence through these experiences have stronger career outcomes .

Georgia Tech isn’t alone. The University System of Georgia has recently created a new role: a chief innovation and entrepreneurial strategies officer to lead an initiative across all of the state’s public colleges and universities.

Other universities are pursuing similar paths, including the University of Virginia , Rice University and Cornell University . All now have an institutionwide leadership position focused on entrepreneurship.

Taken together, these developments suggest that educators increasingly view entrepreneurship as more than just support for students who want to start companies. These steps will help ensure that when students walk across the stage to receive their diplomas, they can meet the challenges ahead of them.

articles.title: What 1,000 years of golden roses tell us about popes’ authority and influence, from Leo IX to Leo XIV
articles.author:
<name>Joëlle Rollo-Koster, Professor Emerita of Medieval History, University of Rhode Island</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/joelle-rollo-koster-1286920"/>
paras: Almost every ceremonial object or ornament of the medieval papal monarchy has disappeared or lost its original purpose. Yet one survives: the golden rose.

On Sept. 26, 2026, during Pope Leo XIV’s visit to France, he traveled to Lourdes, home to one of the world’s most famous shrines to the Virgin Mary. After praying, Leo presented a golden rose to Our Lady of Lourdes – the fifth time he has dedicated a rose to a Marian shrine or image.

The ornate rose Leo offered to Lourdes is not that different from its medieval iterations. The oldest surviving rose is now at the Musée de Cluny in Paris and dates from the early 1300s. Both are golden, with several branches and buds .
Yet who receives the roses, and why, has changed dramatically.

As a medieval historian researching the papacy, I frequently find mentions of the roses. They are ubiquitous in medieval chronicles – most of all, in papal accounting registers . The history of the roses’ beneficiaries reflects the history of the papacy and how its influence has shifted over the centuries.

Most medieval roses were made of gold and silver, adorned with precious stones such as sapphires and rubies. One of the buds formed a small receptacle that held some musk and balsam , rare and expensive fragrances.

The Vatican Apostolic Archives have preserved the accounting registers that itemized many of the roses’ costs. On average, they weighed 11-16 ounces of precious metal and cost the equivalent of 10 years of a laborer’s annual wage .

The golden rose first appeared during the papacy of Leo IX. On April 18, 1049, the pope exempted a nunnery in Alsace – now in Sainte-Croix-en-Plaine, France – from the legal authority and supervision of the local bishop. In return, the head of the nunnery was required to offer the pope a golden rose of some 2 ounces, or of equivalent value. At the time, roses were often used to symbolize a feudal pledge : the submission of a vassal to a lord.

Within a couple of generations, the gift had changed direction: The pope now granted a rose. The first clearly documented case took place in 1096, when Urban II, touring France and preaching the First Crusade, granted it to Fulk of Anjou to reward him for his willingness to participate .

From the 11th century on, the pope offered a rose once a year, on Laetare Sunday : the fourth Sunday of Lent, the period before Easter when many Catholics commit to some form of penance. According to ceremonial books called “ordines ,” the pope held the rose during the worship service, preached about its symbolism, and presented it to a recipient.

On that Sunday, gifting the rose reminded believers that while Lent was difficult, beauty and joy would emerge from it. The day was also a feast in honor of the recipient – typically the prefect of Rome , who supervised the city’s jurisdictions and police.

Eventually, the decision about who should receive the honor rested solely with the pope. Still, it was always bestowed upon those who wielded power: the prefect of Rome, emperors, kings, military leaders and defenders of Christian lands. Receiving the rose was a public acknowledgment that the recipient – usually a warrior – stood beside the pope in protecting the church.

In 1148, for example, Pope Eugene III offered it to the king of Leon and Castile , Alfonso VII. A century later, Pope Innocent IV gave it to Raymond Berenger , count of Provence. In both cases the pope rewarded the fight against Muslims, whom the Vatican saw as “infidels” or heretics.

The Avignon papacy of the 14th century, a period when several popes resided in what is now southern France, accelerated this evolution. Away from Rome, and in the absence of a Roman prefect, the rose’s role as a negotiating tool intensified.

By the 14th century, the ceremony had grown even more elaborate . According to ceremonial books, the pope carried the rose in procession, while its beneficiary held the reins of his horse and kissed the pope’s feet – a gesture of submission.

Historians can estimate how many people received the rose based on evidence available in the Vatican’s accounting registers and other historical records . Over the years, more and more began to be presented to women, and then to shrines. This change shows the history of the papacy – and of its communication strategy. Simply put, the evolution of the rose followed the evolution of papal power itself.

The first few centuries of the rose were a period of conquests and Catholic expansionism, when conversion often came through war. With very few exceptions , roses were offered to commend male medieval rulers, often ones who had militarily defended Catholicism.

The early modern period saw the birth of the Protestant Reformation and many religious conflicts. Popes looked for support from the era’s powerful women rulers, such as Catherine de’ Medici , who played a crucial role during France’s wars of religion between Protestants and Catholics. From the 16th century onward, roses were often given to women like her: empresses, queens and the wives of high dignitaries.
That shift accelerated in the 18th and 19th centuries, when most roses were gifted to Catholic women of high standing. From 1790 to 1893 not a single man received the rose.

This was a period of revolutions and secularization, when the church could not depend on the military leadership of a king, duke or the nobility. Again, queens and empresses dominated the beneficiaries. With the rose, popes could flatter and honor the wives of important rulers, who in turn could pressure their spouses if needed. Eugénie, empress of the French and wife of Napoleon III, received it in 1856 for her piety and philanthropy.

The 20th and 21st centuries saw a total abandonment of gifting the rose to humans. Instead, popes have presented them to shrines and basilicas , typically ones dedicated to the Virgin Mary. The last person given a rose was Charlotte, grand duchess of Luxembourg , who received one in 1956 for her piety and courage during World War II.

Today, Leo XIV continues the tradition . Devotion to Mary remains central to Catholic identity in an age when political authority no longer carries the same religious weight. Gifting the roses to holy shrines, images or basilicas separates them from any suggestion of political and religious alliance or favoritism.

The history of the golden rose reveals the shift of papal priorities from political alliance-building to devotional symbolism . What was once a diplomatic gift addressed to earthly power is now offered to Marian shrines: the roses embody faith itself. The recipients changed because the church’s relationship to power changed .

I see the rose as a perfect example of the Catholic Church’s deep understanding and adaptation to its time and its gift for reinvention. Few institutions have managed to keep a medieval ceremony alive for nearly a millennium while completely transforming its meaning. The golden rose is the papacy’s oldest public relations tool.

articles.title: 2026 midterms could be the end of Pennsylvania’s split legislature, with effects on affordability, election reform, marijuana and more
articles.author:
<name>Daniel J. Mallinson, Associate Professor of Public Policy and Administration, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/daniel-j-mallinson-572958"/>
paras: While many people are paying attention to how the 2026 midterm elections might change the balance of power in Washington, D.C., it is also a potentially pivotal election here in Pennsylvania.

Gov. Josh Shapiro is up for reelection, running against Republican challenger Stacy Garrity, the current state treasurer. Who wins that race will certainly shape the state’s policy agenda for the next two years.

In the General Assembly, which is currently split – Republicans control the Senate and Democrats control the House – both chambers are also up for grabs. Democrats have been slowly eroding the Republicans’ hold over the Senate . In the House, Democrats have a three-seat majority, but Republicans could flip it .
Of course, nationally the wind is at the back of Democrats . Commentators are contemplating the possibility of a Democratic trifecta in Pennsylvania for the first time since 1993 .

I teach public policy at Penn State Harrisburg and have a particular interest in Pennsylvania state politics . I think voters should understand not just the positions of the individual candidates on the ballot, but what the legislative priorities will be for either party if they gain control of the General Assembly.

For a glimpse at potential Democratic priorities should they keep the House and win the Senate, it is helpful to look at what legislation the current Democrat-controlled House has been sending the Republican-controlled Senate.

Election reform has been a perennial priority in the commonwealth since the passage of Act 77 of 2019 and the 2020 election. Act 77 authorized no-excuse absentee balloting and eliminated straight-ticket voting, which was a bipartisan compromise but became a political flash point in President Donald Trump’s efforts to question the 2020 election results. No-excuse means that voters do not need to provide a specific qualifying reason to vote by mail.

Democratic election law priorities have included requiring counties to use ballot drop boxes , maintaining no-excuse mail-in voting , setting clear rules for ballot curing , instituting precanvassing to speed the counting of absentee ballots, and allowing independents to vote in open primary elections .

Gov. Shapiro has repeatedly included revenue projections from adult-use recreational marijuana legalization in his budget proposals, and the House even passed a legalization bill in 2025 . Democrats have said that they will legalize recreational marijuana if they can take the Senate in 2026. But important details of legalization will remain to be worked out, even if Democrats have full control.
Democrats and Republican supporters of legalization disagree as to whether sales should be through private dispensaries or state stores , similar to how alcohol is sold in Pennsylvania.

Social equity measures meant to repair some of the harms of the War on Drugs on communities disproportionately affected by the criminalization of marijuana will also be key to eventual passage. These include things like expungements of past convictions, license set-asides for minority dispensary owners, and community reinvestment of cannabis tax revenues. Even with Democratic control, the devil will be in the details.

Same-sex marriage equality may seem like a settled issue with the 2015 Obergefell v. Hodges decision by the U.S. Supreme Court, but the 2022 overturning of Roe v. Wade by today’s more conservative court has sparked concerns of further changes to precedent.

Pennsylvania’s statutory definition of marriage is still between “one man and one woman,” something that a bipartisan majority in the House tried to change in 2026 to “two individuals.” Democrats are very likely to pick this back up if they win a trifecta. They may even attempt a more durable, but also more procedurally difficult , constitutional amendment that enshrines same-sex marriage rights.

The House has passed several measures to regulate AI and the data center build-out in the commonwealth. This includes a measure that would require warnings on advertisements that were made using AI and several that target energy costs , water use , local government authority and implementing the Governor’s Responsible Infrastructure Development plan. These measures and others are likely to remain on the Democrats’ agenda.
Given that this election is shaping up to be heavily influenced by voters’ concerns about affordability , both parties have the issue on their agendas but will approach it differently.

The Democrats’ Affordability Action Plan includes measures such as property tax and rent rebates, other housing protections for underserved communities, doubling the income tax credit and increasing food and energy security funding.

Another affordability priority for House Democrats since taking control of the chamber in 2023 has been raising the state’s US$7.25 minimum hourly wage over time. The bill passed by the House in March 2026 would have raised it to $11 in 2027, $13 in 2028 and $15 in 2029, with subsequent annual cost-of-living adjustments, if it had been also passed by the Senate. This is important in Philadelphia, given that state law prohibits the city from setting its own minimum wage.
We can turn to the current Republican-controlled Senate for insight into what will be on the party’s agenda if it resumes full control of the Assembly in 2027.

Republicans have also been pushing for election law reform since 2020. In contrast to Democrats, their agenda has included repealing no-excuse absentee balloting , banning the use of ballot drop boxes and instituting stronger voter identification requirements.

Senate Republicans have also been active in proposing and passing AI- and data center-related legislation. A bill banning “nudification” apps, which use AI to remove the clothing from people in pictures and replace them with fake nude images, passed the Senate unanimously in late September.

There has also been bipartisan support for a Republican-proposed ban on the use of nondisclosure agreements in data center development. Republicans in the Senate also proposed designating all of Pennsylvania a Commonwealth Opportunity Zone for AI, which would fast-track data center permits and create a regulatory framework in collaboration with the industry.
While Republican AI legislation is likely to be more enabling of the emergent industry than regulating, Republicans are also concerned about privacy, transparency and costs to their constituents.

Among the costs of data center development are higher energy and water prices . Republicans have already been making energy development a priority, repealing Pennsylvania’s participation in the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative and pushing the governor on his promise of an “ all of the above ” energy strategy.

The stark promise of higher electric prices and poorer grid reliability due to projected data center development in a 2026 Public Utility Commission report is likely to add fuel to Republicans’ push for energy development.

The affordability plan released by House Republicans in March 2026 points to the types of measures the party will pursue if it takes control of the Assembly. A cornerstone is the reduction of taxes , including lowering the personal income tax rate, a temporary elimination of energy and telecommunications taxes, and suspending the state gas tax, which is $0.576 per gallon for gasoline, $0.741 for diesel . Pennsylvania’s gasoline tax is the fifth-highest and the diesel tax is the third-highest in the United States.
A full plan with 10 bills is to be released in coming weeks , but will also include changes to zoning and construction rules to enable faster housing construction.

articles.title: We’ve tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI-generated political ads this year – it’s weird
articles.author:
<name>Travis N. Ridout, Professor of Government and Public Policy, Washington State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/travis-n-ridout-604996"/>
paras: The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people’s televisions and social media feeds.

We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle – using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ad spending – we’ve tracked about US$80 million in spending on almost 170 unique ads that use AI.

What we found has surprised us: AI use spans from hyperrealistic deepfakes to subtle enhancements; Republican sponsors – both candidates and interest groups – are much more likely to use AI than are Democratic sponsors; and, thanks to a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads do not disclose the use of AI at all.

An assortment of politicians and watchdog groups have expressed concern about campaigns using generative AI to produce deepfakes – synthetic videos showing people doing things they did not do – that might deceive voters.

We’ve noticed several ads containing hyperrealistic deepfakes of famous politicians, including Donald Trump , Nancy Pelosi, Barack Obama, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Ocasio-Cortez , in particular, is a favorite among Republican advertisers, appearing in at least five ads.

We’ve seen deepfakes in which a Republican Senate candidate from Louisiana drives a school bus full of undocumented immigrants, a Republican candidate for governor from South Carolina walks arm in arm with drag queens , and an ad in which Liz Cheney, Mitt Romney and Mike Pence are seen carrying pitchforks on the White House lawn.

People who are not politicians made appearances, too, including a fake Dr. Anthony Fauci , seen running around a state fair with a huge syringe, presumably eager to vaccinate everyone. We’ve also noticed several ads in which AI was used to generate crowds or constituents .

In several cases, AI was used to enhance visuals rather than generate something new. One ad from Chip Keating, a Republican candidate for governor in Oklahoma, includes an AI disclaimer , but it doesn’t specify exactly how AI was used. Ads that use AI to enhance visuals don’t necessarily look different from ads that were created in the pre-AI era, which makes it difficult for viewers to discern whether they depict something false.
Republicans – both candidates and groups such as super PACs and 501(c) organizations – are much more likely to use AI in their ads than are Democrats, according to our research.
In fact, Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups were behind 80% of the ads we tracked and 83% of the spending .

We can only speculate as to why Republicans dominate the use of AI in political advertising in 2026. In general, Democrats tend to take on a regulatory mindset when it comes to political campaigns, favoring limits on campaign spending and required disclosures. In 2022, for instance, only Senate Democrats and two independents voted to advance the DISCLOSE Act that would have required additional campaign finance disclosures for super PACs, labor unions and corporations. Republicans, by contrast, tend to be more in favor of a free market approach .

These more general philosophies may be reflected in the parties’ use of generative AI for political advertising, something about which voters are worried. Polling shows broad support for more regulation , with 78% of registered voters favoring a ban on AI content that makes deceptive claims about candidates.

Because regulation of AI in advertising depends on a patchwork of state legislation , many of these ads are not required to disclose the use of AI. This lack of disclaimers makes tracking AI use in ads challenging. Our team has relied on media coverage and trained student coders to flag ads that are potentially AI-generated.

Across 35 states, only 31% of the ads we tracked – representing 22% of the spending – disclosed the use of AI tools. The wording of these disclaimers was all over the map. For example, one Georgia ad included the disclaimer, “This video has been manipulated or generated with artificial intelligence,” while an Oklahoma ad said, “Political satire. AI-generated images do not depict actual events.” A North Carolina state Senate ad said, “You guessed it! AI was definitely used to generate these silly video clips.”

Some advertisers voluntarily disclose the use of AI even when they are not required to do so. Sometimes, the opposite occurs – advertisers don’t include disclaimers even when state law requires them to. In fact, we’ve found that a state law that requires disclaimers on ads that use AI has very little relationship with the actual use of disclaimers.

In states without laws governing the use of AI in political ads, 32% of ads contained a disclaimer; by contrast, in states with laws governing the use of AI, 29% contained a disclaimer. This comparison, however, is not perfect, as some of the ads in our database aren’t covered by their state’s law. Some states, such as Colorado, have laws that apply only to candidate deepfakes and thus exclude other uses of AI. In other instances, such as in Louisiana, an AI law was enacted after the ad aired.

Minnesota law generally bans deepfakes in political ads, but an ad featuring synthetic video of Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan aired in May 2026 anyway. Whether it violated state law is uncertain, as the law requires that the media be “so realistic that a reasonable person would believe it depicts speech or conduct of an individual who did not in fact engage in such speech or conduct.”
Moving forward, the real policy challenge will revolve around transparency, the enforceability of existing laws and simply figuring out what type of disclosure would be helpful to voters.

articles.title: Nathan Vass’ Deciding to See: Washington State Book Awards Finalist
articles.author: Nathan Vass
paras: We urban planning and transit enthusiasts tend not to think of the street in terms of narrative. Most of the literature we digest on these favorite subjects of ours – the opening of a new train line, the behind-the-scenes of a housing development, the political importance of this or that measure and its effects – is in the form of articles or video essays, which have the luxury of being instantly producible, with up-to-the-minute observations and (ideally) journalism’s commitment to a minimum of editorializing. We think of journalism as the primary method of which to conceive of the street.

A 300-page book which took five years to write might seem an odd fit for the above landscape, especially a book that can’t be called journalism, even if it is nonfiction. But I think humans ultimately conceive of everything in terms of narrative.

We think of our days and our projects and our entire lives as stories, with arcs, in which we (of course) are the protagonist. We wish for happy endings, or at least edifying ones, and if we don’t get them we tell ourselves the story isn’t over yet. We are linear, time-based creatures, and in the same way we search for a story when watching one of the time-based art forms, even when there may not be one there at all (like dance), we frame how we think about our lives using the rules of narrative.

I think stories are the most powerful way to communicate. Paul Currington says opinions divide people; stories bring them together. In our (dis)information age, facts, or assertions masquerading as facts, have shown themselves to have limited value in changing minds.

If your family member is prejudiced, they won’t come around to your perspective when you dump data in their lap explaining how racism or sexism are shortsighted. They’ll come around because of primary experience happening in the one story they do care about, their own , the story of their life, as they get to know their coworker who’s from somewhere far away, or their friend’s child, who lives by different rules. The human element.

I didn’t write either of my books to change people’s minds. I wrote them to share a world I find interesting and underrepresented in the world of literature. I wrote them because there was so much life happening in this “lowbrow” space of unglamorous liminal life, so dense with incident and color and laughter and sorrow, and so few artists were transposing it to the “highbrow” space of probing literary reflection, of the word as art form.

I know there are others like me, but maybe too many of our great authors stay inside their offices, and too many of our best bus drivers don’t study comparative literature. Can I help it if I have interests and passions which have nothing to do with each other??

We know the power of stories, and we know the joy of sharing bus stories, which we humans will never stop telling each other, not as long as there’s transit in our lives. I’m frankly floored by the success my latest book continues to have – continuously bestselling in our city for over a year now, taught as a textbook at Seattle U, and now a Finalist for the 2026 Washington State Book Awards , alongside Rebecca Brown (Eep eep! I can die happy now) and others… all of this is thanks to you readers and enthusiasts, especially transit enthusiasts.

The Urbanist 's readers are my ideal audience: those of us interested in living as an urban collective, curious to see how the world of the street looks when viewed through the lens of art and narrative, searching for how we can live in the same forward direction, part of the same common project.

paras: Some climate tech startups tied to the AI boom are still attracting investors, but deals are fewer overall and times are tougher for companies addressing sustainability issues that don’t align with data center needs.

Concerns about those trends inspired a one-time Washington state initiative called the Opalene Climate Challenge , which was led by the nonprofit VertueLab . The effort announced six investments from a pool of nearly 40 applicants.

The program planned to partner with the state to secure matching dollars, but organizers realized it would take too long to raise the needed capital. Instead, they relied solely on philanthropic donors.

“The imperative was to get the money out to these climate tech startups who are doing extraordinary work but are confronting that pinch in capital,” said Allison Arnold, co-director of the Opalene Climate Challenge.

Sustainability startups that develop hardware or physical products can face a more difficult path to scale than software companies because they typically require more capital, longer development cycles and time-consuming work to manufacture, test and deploy their technologies.

The challenge aimed to fill an early-stage funding gap with recoverable grants from donor-advised funds. Successful investments will return proceeds to the donor’s fund or another designated nonprofit.

Five of the six winners are commercializing technologies developed at the University of Washington or Washington State University. Many of the startups have participated in mentoring programs such as the Cascadia Clean Tech Accelerator or UW’s CoMotion Labs Climate Tech Incubator, or received investments from the E8 angel group.

“Those entrepreneurs who have actively sought out the resources in our ecosystem have had greater success. For most companies, it takes more than just the money,” Arnold said. At the same time, she added, “money is what has been missing in our corner of the country. We don’t have the type of risk capital that’s available in places like Silicon Valley, Boston or New York.”

articles.title: Seattle and San Francisco: Big tech, political backlash and the AI boom
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Tech remade Seattle and San Francisco over the past three decades, bringing jobs and wealth along with soaring housing costs and a political backlash. Now the AI boom is hitting both cities, before either has resolved the tensions that have repeatedly divided their communities.

That’s the subject of this week’s GeekWire Podcast, a live joint taping with the Blue City Blues podcast at the National Nordic Museum in Seattle. GeekWire co-founder John Cook joins historian Margaret O’Mara, author of “ The Code ,” and San Francisco journalist Jonathan Weber, author of “ City on the Edge ,” with Blue City Blues hosts David Hyde and Sandeep Kaushik.
Here are some of the key takeaways from the conversation.
The tech industry’s conflicts in Seattle and San Francisco began when the industry moved out of the suburbs and into the middle of both cities.
Silicon Valley grew up 30 to 40 miles south of San Francisco, and Microsoft built a suburban campus in Redmond that O’Mara called “its own kind of bubble far away from the city.”

When Weber arrived in San Francisco in 1990 to cover Silicon Valley for the Los Angeles Times, he said, “there was essentially no tech in the city at all.” That changed with the dot-com boom, which brought the first backlash in San Francisco’s Mission District in the late 1990s.

In Seattle, a similar shift happened with Amazon’s move to South Lake Union, starting in 2010. John said Amazon was “most perfectly positioned” at its earlier headquarters on Beacon Hill, southeast of downtown Seattle, “completely isolated from the rest of the city.”

“When things really shifted for Amazon is when they decided to plant themselves in the middle of the city,” John said. “Then things accelerate, and then these problems start to come in, and Amazon starts to get blamed.”
The tech industry grew up in an era of low taxes and light regulation, and that’s baked into its business model.

O’Mara pointed to 1978, when California voters passed Proposition 13, which capped property taxes and “essentially starved localities of revenue,” she said. Personal computers and video games were taking off in that same era. “Silicon Valley’s kind of grown up in that world,” she said.

In Seattle, John said, Amazon’s view was that it was doing enough by bringing jobs to the city, while the city’s progressive leaders wanted more as prices rose. “Those two philosophies just collided in Seattle in real time,” he said.
Cities have limited leverage, Weber said. “A company can move two miles and avoid whatever taxes the city wants to impose.”
Seattle’s tech and business leaders, unhappy with the city’s political leadership, are organizing to fill the gap themselves.

Asked whether tech leaders think they’ve been getting good leadership from Seattle’s mayors, John said, “Short answer: No.” Businesses feel they’re paying a growing list of new taxes, he said, without seeing results on basics like potholes and clean streets.

In recent months, business figures including Microsoft’s Brad Smith, former Gov. Chris Gregoire and Joe Nguyen of the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce have started forming coalitions and pooling their resources. “They’re going on offense,” John said. “They feel there’s a vacuum and a gap here based on this lack of political leadership.”
John said one of a mayor’s big jobs is to be “the chief cheerleader of the region and the city,” and Seattle’s recent mayors haven’t done it.
Weber said San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie has made that role a big part of his success: “Even though he’s a billionaire, he comes across as kind of a regular San Francisco guy.”
“That’s kind of a regular San Francisco guy these days,” O’Mara quipped.
San Francisco is the center of the AI boom, but Seattle and the Bay Area have always depended on each other more than they’ve competed.
Weber called San Francisco the undisputed capital of AI, as the home of OpenAI and Anthropic. The boom has brought so much wealth to the city, he said, that “there’s a mansion shortage.”

John said the gap between the two regions in venture funding for AI is “an astronomical difference.” But OpenAI and Anthropic have both opened engineering centers in the Seattle area, he said, hiring people who don’t want to leave.
Microsoft and Amazon both raised early money from Bay Area venture capitalists, O’Mara said.

John cited the longtime advice for Seattle founders: “Start your company and build your company in Seattle, raise your money in the Bay Area.” But Seattle has always run second to the Bay Area, John said, and that’s OK. “Who cares?” he said. “They are their own thing. We’re our own thing.”
The Gilded Age offers a precedent for putting guardrails on AI.

O’Mara compared the moment to the era of Carnegie and Rockefeller, when fast-growing industries overwhelmed a small U.S. government, and the regulation that followed still left room to make a lot of money.
Overemphasizing the novelty of AI, she said, “becomes a very convenient excuse not to regulate it.”

Weber said the AI debate is hard to read because most of the people in it are “talking their book,” with a business interest in the positions they take. The issue is arising, he said, at a time when “we essentially don’t have any national political leadership that’s able to deal with it.”
“So many things are indeed new,” O’Mara said, “but it doesn’t mean that nothing can be done.”
Both cities need to protect their quality of place, and tech itself can undermine it.

O’Mara said building a tech hub comes down to three things: capital, institutions such as research universities, and quality of place. Asked what Seattle and San Francisco should do differently over the next decade, she picked the third.
“This is not just making things nice for Amazon engineers getting paid $300,000 a year,” O’Mara said. “It is making the city safe, vital and fun.”

Weber said tech threatens that sense of place, because people who can shop, meet and find entertainment online don’t need the city in the same way. In San Francisco’s traditional nightlife districts, he said, there’s little going on after 9 p.m., while the city’s caterers and party planners are busy. “A lot of social life has moved indoors into private spaces,” he said.
To which John joked, “I just want to enjoy San Francisco in the metaverse.”

articles.title: Op-Ed: Fill in the Spring Boulevard Gap with a Trail
articles.author: Eastside Urbanism
paras: Do arterial roads belong in city parks? That is one of the key questions the Bellevue City Council will need to consider during its October 6 budget deliberations on transportation projects. The staff has presented an option to give full funding (for the first time) of $74.8 million to the one-third-mile, two-lane Spring Boulevard “gap” with a new 0.1% sales tax . But this "Zone 3" plan is colliding with another emerging project on the same land: the BelRed Neighborhood Park .

We believe roads like that do not belong in a park. The City should instead plan a pedestrian/bicycle-only trail. But before we make that case, let’s step back to understand the historical precedents and the reasons the City wants to build the road.

Bellevue, the self-described “City in a Park,” has many beautiful parks, such as Bannerwood, Crossroads, Downtown, Highland, Lake Hills, Lakemont, Mercer Slough, Meydenbauer, Robinswood, Surrey Downs, Weowna, and Wilburton Hill. The fact that none of these parks have arterial roads going through them shows Bellevue residents have been prioritizing parks over cars for as long as the city has existed.

Wilburton Hill Park presents a particularly enticing cut-through opportunity to extend 124th Ave south of Main St to the Lake Hills Connector. The City considered this project many years ago, but it was so forcefully rejected by residents that the policy to not do it is now cemented as S-WI-15 in the Wilburton subarea plan .

Downtown Park is another interesting case to examine. Before building that park in the mid 1980s, the City removed a large section of 102nd Avenue, which had bisected the site for decades. As a video from the time makes clear, the City wanted to create a big, green meadow that would last forever, and it would have been unthinkable to compromise that vision for a few seconds of driver convenience.

Downtown Bellevue of the 1980’s, like BelRed today , was a mostly commercial district just beginning its journey to the mixed-use, high-rise urban center it is now. The successful Downtown Park strategy of prioritizing urban green space provides a model worthy of replication in BelRed.

So if Bellevue has never allowed arterials in parks in the past, then why is it planning to do so now? The City laid out the purpose of Spring Boulevard's Zone 3 in an application for a federal grant in 2024. According to the City, the project would:

We dispute the 2-3 minute reduction for drivers. Google Maps estimates the total driving time for the existing route along BelRed Road at just two minutes , so the reduction in driving time would be even less. Also, cars on the new route would often need to yield at crosswalks in the busy park, further eroding any small improvement in driving times.

Apart from that exaggerated driving time reduction, all of the other justifications for the project would also apply to a trail. In fact, if the City wants to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a trail would be better than a road because it would be more effective at encouraging travel by bicycle without creating the infamous induced traffic demand associated with new roads. And if the City wants to attract investment, a park without an arterial would be more appealing to residents, and therefore more attractive for housing developers and employers.

The Spring Boulevard plan was initially presented to the City Council in 2011. At that time, there were plans for another large park in BelRed . It was tentatively called Northup Meadows, and it would have been on the site of what instead became Sound Transit’s train base . Since the plan for that park fell apart, the other BelRed park (in Spring Boulevard’s path) has gained a new degree of importance as the only park in the rapidly-growing area. It is only appropriate to re-evaluate the need for Spring Boulevard (Zone 3) in light of the significantly changed conditions.
To put our case simply: BelRed Park is a wonderful idea and letting drivers cut through would wreck it.

Parents visiting the park would need to constantly worry about safety as distracted drivers speed by. Their kids couldn’t roam freely and play. Picnicking families would have to put up with constant road noise and backfiring car exhausts. Green grass would cede to hot asphalt. Even with a crosswalk or two, people would try to cross the road everywhere, a recipe for pedestrian injuries. Being close to light rail stations could make BelRed Park one of the best outdoor event spaces in the city, but nobody wants a bunch of loud cars cutting through their event.

Now let’s talk about money. Spring Boulevard's Zone 3 project would cost about $75 million . Last year, Bellevue staff estimated a trail cost at $18-20 million ( on page 12 of these minutes ). In other words, about 75% of the project budget would be directed exclusively at the goal of trying to save drivers a few seconds of travel time.

With a trail, all of the City’s other goals could be achieved at 25% the cost. (Since most of that cost is for land acquisition, and the land owner is Sound Transit , who has been supportive of parks and pedestrian infrastructure around their stations, we might be able to save even more money by making a deal with Sound Transit to put a trail on their land without buying it.)

Think about your favorite park. Now imagine what it would be like with an arterial road going directly through it. That’s what the Spring Boulevard Zone 3 project would do to BelRed Park, before it even has a chance to show how great it can be.

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Salmon SEEson
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: Every year, thousands of salmon travel though creeks, rivers and lakes in King County on their return trip from the ocean. These adult salmon return to fresh water to spawn the next generation. The county’s Salmon SEEson program, now in its 20th year, highlights the habitat restoration, stormwater management, and community stewardship that ensure the fish can complete their journey. The program also highlights some of the best locations for watching the great salmon migration. An interactive map is available here .

One of the primary dangers to coho salmon in King County’s streams and rivers is a chemical from car tires . A chemical called 6PPD is used in almost all tires to protect them from ground-level ozone. When ozone reacts with 6PPD, it creates a toxic chemical called 6PPD-quinone. 6PPD-quinone is left on the roadway and washed into nearby waterways during the next rain. Some locations have a stormwater filter to prevent 6PPD-quinone from entering a waterway, but these systems cannot be built for every road.

To avoid adding more 6PPD-quinone to the salmon’s habitat, do not drive to see the salmon migration. Instead, ride the bus! EcoCity Action has organized a few transit trips to see salmon. articles.title: Op-Ed: Seattle’s Utility Fee Policy Echoes Redlining
articles.author: Donna Breske (Guest Contributor)
paras: Seattle’s permitting policies for new housing requires that applicants pay for public infrastructure upgrades within historically marginalized neighborhoods that are not required of applicants in more affluent neighborhoods.

Redlined communities faced policies, including the denial of access to home loans that restricted home ownership and affordable housing. Two current Seattle permitting policies for new-home construction continue this inequitable treatment.

Despite Seattle’s official commitments on racial justice and social equity, inequitable outcomes are embedded within the sidewalk and water service policies and fees associated with new home construction. The outcome for many marginalized communities is increased costs, which could exceed those in more affluent communities by $350,000 for the same type of project.

The Seattle Municipal Code has a two-tiered sidewalk policy. The code gives relief for housing projects outside of Urban Centers, while no such relief is afforded to the projects within. This relief applies to projects of nine units or less. For those small projects required to install sidewalks, the cost can be upwards of $100,000.

Since Seattle has designated the lion’s share of its Urban Centers in historically “red-lined” communities, there is a social equity disparity that is reflected in the Seattle Sidewalk Code. Relief is provided to more affluent communities, however no such relief to historically marginalized communities.

A better solution may be to change the Seattle Municipal Code to allow the option for payment of a reasonable fee-in-lieu-of sidewalk construction. This will facilitate equitable relief regardless of the location of the project within the City. The money collected could be applied to areas of the city with the highest need for sidewalks.

Another disparity appears in Seattle Public Utilities’ (SPU’s) water-service policy WTR-440. It applies to a water main that runs primarily through historically marginalized communities and is installed within Beacon Avenue and extends north and continues under 21st Avenue S.
The policy requires permit applicants whose property is on a street where the supply main is located to pay for and install a large valve at a total cost around $250,000.

Furthermore, Seattle’s supply main is located within communities that are also designated as Design Review Equity Areas . Outreach to these communities is required to ensure that they have a meaningful voice in projects affecting them. These Design Review Areas coincide with historically redlined areas.

One neighborhood in the North Rainier Urban Hub, has seen five small housing proposals unable to proceed. Numerous projects along Beacon Avenue have come to an abrupt halt once the project proponent is informed of the valve requirement. Small projects have no economy of scale to pay the $250,000 estimated cost. Small-scale homebuilders are not suited to perform major public works water system upgrades and the end result is unrealized housing and ongoing social inequity.

Not all permitting barriers include a social inequity component. Moreover, permitting policies that affect housing outcomes do extend beyond Seattle to many jurisdictions throughout the Puget Sound region.
Barriers run the gamut and include storm water policy, road network, strict floor area ratio requirements that limit housing capacity, critical area interpretations, and more.

Learn how permitting policies throughout the region are affecting housing production and join in on the conversation to find solutions by attending my Permit Barriers Symposium on October 15 at Seattle University.

articles.title: Scores Turn Out To Celebrate Sound Transit's First Infill Station
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: What had been billed as a "small community event" turned into a major party Wednesday as hundreds of transit fans converged on Sound Transit's newest light rail station in North Seattle to celebrate its grand opening. Pinehurst Station , perched over I-5 near NE 130th Street, is the agency's first infill station, a stop added along an existing line.

"It was a joyous occasion with people walking, biking, and rolling to check out their new mobility option, including many arriving on King County Metro's new Route 77, which provides a direct and convenient connection to the station," Sound Transit CEO Dow Constantine said the following day at a board committee meeting.

Sound Transit had undeniably treated the opening of Pinehurst Station as a subdued affair, in the wake of full line openings where the agency pulled out all the stops. Unlike past major light rail openings, the start of service happened on a weekday, meeting the agency's promise of getting the station open in the third quarter of the year. A ribbon cutting occurred the night before, separating the elected officials celebrating the station from the throngs of riders checking it out.

Just one food truck was on hand to provide sustenance for hundreds, at a station that is fairly isolated from other restaurants, and the Sound Transit pop-up shop on hand selling custom Pinehurst merch started running out of inventory fairly quickly.

But none of that seemed to faze transit lovers who converged on the station plaza by the hundreds, with many standing in an epic line that stretched back to 130th Street for a chance to win a Boop collectible. (Don't know Boop? You've been missing out. )

Other attendees listened to live music or participated in art making activities with Romson Bustillo, the very same artist who created the artwork adorning Pinehurst Station – porcelain enamel paintings that wrap around the side of the building into its main entrance from 130th. Bustillo's booth was popular with kids who could make their own art projects to take home as souvenirs.

But most who stopped by were there to check out the station itself, which had originally not been set to open until 2031, moved up in order to take advantage of the ability to do work concurrently with the broader Lynnwood Link extension. While that line ultimately beat Pinehurst to a ribbon-cutting by more than two years, the ability to do work before that happened ultimately saved riders headaches in addition to being cheaper for Sound Transit.

As Sound Transit's festival wrapped up, a group of around 50 joined for The Urbanist's walking tour of the neighborhood. The tour used the Jackson Park Perimeter Trail to explore the fenced edge of the golf course, before turning south on 15th Avenue NE to visit the fledgling business district. The tour turned back toward the station via NE 125th Street to take in the new protected bike lane and roundabout intersection with Roosevelt Way.

Along the way, James Wu and Shirley Leung of EcoCity Action told tour participants about their group's campaign to reimagine Jackson Park Golf Course . One core idea: making it possible for people to walk through the 160-acre park and get more use out it, such as by adding picnic areas or soccer pitches or basketball courts. Some have even proposed housing , although that's not part of the current campaign given obstacles like zoning and restrictions on reusing park land.

Pinehurst organizer Renee Staton recounted the history of local grassroots advocacy that forced the station into agency plans and accelerated its timeline. Staton said most of her neighbors support the City's plan to upzone Pinehurst's single family areas to allow more housing, and she's pushing to move up the timeline ahead of delayed Comprehensive Plan changes.

Pinehurst has attracted attention for its price tag – $240 million, up from an initial 2020 estimate of $144 million – and its adjacent land use, primarily single-family homes, I-5, and a large, city-owned golf course. One-term Sammamish councilmember (and talk radio host) John Curley called the station a " a total waste of money " and asserted its construction was "criminal."

On the low end, Pinehurst is expected to see around 1,100 daily riders, increasing to as many as 4,200 as Sound Transit fully builds out its light rail network, and the City of Seattle hopefully brings in some additional residential density onto the surrounding blocks.

While Seattle urbanists would certainly love to see Pinehurst embedded into a highrise district, that's not what exists between Northgate and South Shoreline today. When so often the argument around adding density comes up, a lack of infrastructure is cited as a reason to back away, and yet when the infrastructure comes first, it becomes a waste of money.

As far as costs go, it's undeniable that the station is pricey. But as an infill station along an elevated line, $240 million is a steal relative to other Sound Transit projects, only a little more than the at-grade Graham Street infill station in the Rainier Valley at $214 million. The elevated Boeing Access Road Station in Tukwila, so expensive that it was not able to fit into Sound Transit's newly aligned ST3 plan after adjustments were made to account for a $34.5 billion shortfall, is expected to cost as much as $475 million .

One of the biggest value adds right now from Pinehurst come from its ability to act as a bus transfer spot, easier for Metro to access from neighborhoods like Lake City and Bitter Lake than either Shoreline South or Northgate. NE 130th Street, being remade right now by the Seattle Department of Transportation to feature protected bike lanes connecting right with the station, is much improved from its state just a few years ago.

Haters going to hate, but ultimately allowing riders in 2026 to access Pinehurst Station, years ahead of schedule, is a major win for transit in Puget Sound. And the crowds that turned out Wednesday to celebrate the day are a testament to that fact.

articles.title: Kink Center wants Capitol Hill to know it’s mostly about the ‘center’
articles.author: AGPhoto
paras: Walk past the E Pike sidewalk sign for Kink Center and you might expect something out of a dirty movie.
Step inside on a typical night and you’re more likely to find a board game in progress, a book club mid-debate, or somebody passing around cupcakes.
“I think that people see these opening scenes of The Matrix as the idea for what a kink club looks like,” said Raven Dubh , the volunteer-run venue’s executive director.
“… and we’re just in here eating cupcakes.”

That gap between expectation and reality is kind of the point. Kink Center opened last year as what its organizers call a third space, a community center first, oriented toward kink and queer folks and built around accessibility.

Dubh says the idea grew out of need. Seattle has some good options for kink events, but few built around the accessibility the team wanted, and almost none affordable enough for a beginning organizer to take a swing.
“It’s a very expensive failure if you try somewhere else,” Dubh said.
Dubh said friends trying to organize their own events ran into cost and resource challenges.
“The more I was trying to help people do that, I realized they couldn’t,” Dubh said. “They couldn’t front that kind of money.”
Accessibility at the center takes many forms: masking and clean-air policies with HEPA filtration, ADA-accessible bathrooms and elevator access, rental rates kept low so tickets can be cheap or free.
“The barrier to entry is so low, and so many people can try, and the cost if it doesn’t work out isn’t so high for them,” said Luna , the volunteer-run venue’s director of marketing.

Most of what happens here is about getting together and talking. Socials fill the bulk of the calendar, Luna said, followed by classes, “We found a really big thirst to learn in the community”, and then parties, including the center’s own Masked Mayhem. Outside groups rent the space for everything from kink events to birthday parties to company holiday parties, as long as they follow the venue’s posted guidelines.

Neighbors, by the team’s account, have been supportive. Luna said the center has a good relationship with nearby businesses, including downstairs neighbor A/stir it taps for catering. And on a Hill that’s also home to shops like Doghouse Leathers , the sign out front rarely raises eyebrows.
“People see the Kink Center sign, and maybe they don’t frequent Cap Hill,” Luna said. “And they just go, ‘That’s Cap Hill.'”
Luna sees the center as a natural extension of the neighborhood’s queer, sex-positive history.
For Dubh, it’s about normalizing. “It’s not an us versus them,” Dubh said. “It’s a part of that person’s life, and as much as we can normalize that into society, that should be our north star.”
That’s why the calendar includes book clubs and meetups that have little to do with kink.
“When we say third space for kink people, that’s what we mean,” Dubh said. “There are things you can do here because you are part of a community. It doesn’t have to be kink.”

Kink Center is volunteer-run and furnished almost entirely with donated furniture. Dubh, who works in tech, has covered much of the gap personally. This year, the center shifted to asking for small monthly donations, $1 or $2, which made budgeting more predictable. Dubh said the amount they cover out of pocket each month has dropped “pretty dramatically.”
“Every dollar counts,” Dubh said, including the couple of bucks folks donate at events.

The next goal is expanding into the other half of the building. The current layout limits most events around 50 to 75 people. Opening the wall would allow 100-person classes, cheaper tickets, better pay for educators, and events the current shape can’t fit.
“We sell out a lot of our classes, and we wish we could just have an extra 20 or 30 seats,” Dubh said. What’s holding it back? “It’s just money.”

Who’s behind it? The answer, Luna said, is regular people, including volunteers who work the door for an hour and head home, “because all they wanted to do was help at the door for an hour and contribute to their community in that way.”

Dubh said the team’s queerness shows up in how decisions get made: varied backgrounds, ideas Dubh never would have reached alone, and directors empowered to push back. Dubh doesn’t even want to stay on the board long-term. “I want to be punted out so fast,” Dubh said.

Luna said the table feels level. “Grace is always given because we are all focused and aligned on the same goal, which is providing a space to the community that is accessible and feels good for everybody.”

For the kink-curious, both recommend starting small with a social or a munch, like the board game munch the center hosts twice a month. Dubh said the Seattle Freeze actually works in newcomers’ favor.
“If you go to an event and just don’t socialize, it’s kind of expected,” Dubh said. “You just existed in the space, and that is a big step one.”
“Everyone was new once,” Luna said. “That’s what we’re all doing this for.”
“Kink Center as a name, it’s actually backwards in terms of our priority,” Dubh said. “Third space first.”
Kink Center is located at 814 E Pike. Learn more at kinkcenter.org .

CORRECTIONS : We have updated this report to correct a quote that was accidentally misattributed to the incorrect speaker. We also screwed up the address. The Kink Center is at 814 E Pike — not at 816.
